column14: While Publicis leads peers via proprietary Epsilon identity data and Sapient digital transformation, 5-year median GAAP ROIC hovers around 8.5–9.1%, well below the 12% hurdle due to past acquisition goodwill. Agency fee models face continuous procurement scrutiny and client in-housing threats, lacking pricing power >= inflation.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & lacks above-inflation pricing power, REJECT). Publicis is the best-performing global advertising holdco, but historical GAAP ROIC of 8.5–9.1% fails the 12% Munger bar due to acquisition intangibles (€4.4B Epsilon, €3.7B Sapient). Agency contracts face constant procurement re-tendering and in-housing, precluding durable pricing power above inflation.
column21: Publicis Groupe reported operating margins of 18.0–18.2% and annual FCF before working capital of €1.7B–€2.0B across 2022–2025. However, GAAP ROIC remains depressed at ~8.5–9.1% against a WACC of ~9.3%, burdened by €10B+ in goodwill and intangibles. Client marketing budgets are cyclical, and holding company media buying faces disintermediation from direct tech platforms and generative AI creative tools.

column14: Media-buying scale and legacy agency-of-record relationships have been systematically disintermediated by platform self-serve tools (Google, Meta, Amazon) and client in-housing. Historical GAAP ROIC of 6–8% (dropping to ~3% in 2023) is far below the 12% hurdle, with negative pricing power.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & negative pricing power, REJECT). WPP suffers from a multi-decade rollup legacy burdened with goodwill, generating sub-8% multi-year median GAAP ROIC. Media-buying scale advantages have eroded as clients build internal marketing teams, switch to programmatic self-serve platforms, and demand fee reductions.
column21: WPP reported ROIC of 11.4% (2022), 3.4% (2023), and ~8-10% (2024), yielding a 5-year median well below 10%. Operating margins lag top peers at 11–14%. Ongoing marquee account re-pitches, fee deflation, and restructuring charges highlight the lack of economic moat and absence of above-inflation pricing power.

column11: Non-essential / easily forgone product or service; linear broadcast viewing and spot TV ads face structural substitution from global streaming and digital platforms.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Non-essential broadcast ad model facing structural substitution, REJECT). Free-to-air commercial linear broadcasting is neither an essential Western need nor an enduring Lindy everyday habit. Spot television advertising is easily deferred or substituted for digital video and search, while viewers continuously migrate away to global on-demand streamers.
column21: ITV Total Advertising Revenue (TAR) remains cyclical and volatile (£1,957M in 2022 down to ~£1,820M in 2024). Linear audiences continue a secular decline toward YouTube, TikTok, Netflix, and Disney+. While ITV Studios content production is healthier (£2.0B revenue), it requires heavy working capital and talent commitments, and ITVX remains subscale against global streaming giants.

column14: Ofcom regulatory price caps on Openreach wholesale broadband access, combined with aggressive altnet fiber overbuilding (CityFibre, Hyperoptic) and ongoing legacy copper line losses, compress returns. GAAP ROIC of 6–7% and ROCE of 8.3–8.5% fall far short of the 12% hurdle.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & regulated wholesale price caps, REJECT). Openreach represents critical national UK infrastructure, but Ofcom price controls and fierce altnet fiber competition structurally suppress returns on invested capital to 6–7% (ROCE 8.3–8.5%). Heavy multi-billion FTTP capex, £19B+ net debt, and pension obligations leave zero pricing power above inflation.
column21: BT Group reported ROCE of 8.3% (FY23) and 8.5% (FY24), with independent ROIC estimated at ~6-7%, failing the 12% Munger threshold. FTTP buildout to 25 million homes consumes £5B+ in annual capex while Openreach faces net broadband line losses to competitive altnets. Regulated wholesale access formulas prevent real above-inflation pricing.

column14: Despite T-Mobile US's 5G mid-band spectrum leadership and German fixed broadband dominance, 4-year median GAAP ROIC is 11.57% (failing 12%). T-Mobile's foundational 'Price-Lock' guarantee and German regulatory wholesale price caps prevent pricing power >= inflation across full business cycles.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & lacks above-inflation pricing power, REJECT). Deutsche Telekom is an exceptional transatlantic telecom operator driven by T-Mobile US, but 4-year median GAAP ROIC of 11.57% falls short of the 12% hurdle. T-Mobile's Price-Lock marketing guarantee and German regulatory rate constraints prevent above-inflation pricing, while €96B in debt violates fortress standards.
column21: Reported GAAP ROIC averaged 11.57% across 2022–2025 (10.05% in 2022, 9.54% in 2023, 15.51% in 2024, 13.08% in 2025). LT Debt of €96.0B creates 9.2x Net Debt / NI leverage and interest coverage of 3.98x (EBIT €26.0B vs Interest €6.55B), below the 5.0x fortress threshold. Annual capex exceeds €19B.

column14: While Elisa achieves stellar capital efficiency for a telecom (17.7% median GAAP ROIC, ~48% tangible ROIC) via network automation and software, mature Finnish unlimited-data plan competition prevented above-inflation pricing: nominal Owner EPS declined -1.2%/yr over 2022–2025 during >16% cumulative Eurozone inflation.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Lacks above-inflation pricing power, REJECT). Europe's highest-quality, best-managed telco with 17.7% ROIC and >100% cash conversion, but fails Gate 3b as mature Finnish telecom subscriptions could not keep pace with 2022–2025 inflation (nominal Owner EPS fell -1.2%/yr despite >16% cumulative inflation).
column21: Reported GAAP ROIC of 16.5–18.1% (median 17.65%) and FCF conversion of 102% demonstrate industry-leading operational excellence. However, Net Income fell from €374M in 2022 to €342M in 2025 and Owner EPS declined from €2.33 to €2.25 despite >16% Eurozone inflation, proving that fierce 3-player domestic competition caps real pricing power.

column11: Primary listing in Greece is outside approved rule-of-law Western developed markets (in_market == 'N') with elevated sovereign, macroeconomic, and regulatory risk.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (gate_2 = 'N', REJECT). Primary listing and operations in Greece are outside approved Western developed markets (in_market == 'N'). Greek telecom incumbent (Deutsche Telekom-controlled) operates in a mature, low-growth market subject to historical sovereign and regulatory volatility.
column21: OTE holds leading market share in Greek fixed broadband and mobile telephony under Deutsche Telekom governance. However, the listing country (Greece) is excluded from the approved rule-of-law Western developed market universe (in_market == 'N'), triggering an automatic Gate 2 rejection.

column14: KPN owns nationwide fixed fiber and mobile infrastructure in the Netherlands, but regulated wholesale access and three-player competition (VodafoneZiggo, Odido) cap pricing power below inflation, resulting in flat 2022-2025 net income and sub-2% Owner EPS CAGR.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (gate_3b_pricing_and_proof = 'N', REJECT). Regulated wholesale access and intense three-player competition (VodafoneZiggo, Odido) cap real pricing power below inflation, holding Owner EPS CAGR to ~2% over 2022-2025 despite fiber rollout and share buybacks.
column21: KPN operates nationwide Dutch fixed and mobile networks with 12.4% median GAAP ROIC and ~19% tangible ROIC. However, revenue grew just 2.9% p.a. from 2022 to 2025 while cumulative Dutch inflation exceeded 17%, and net income remained flat at €800m. Promotional discounting and regulatory wholesale rate scrutiny eliminate pricing power >= inflation.

column14: Nationwide fiber and mobile physical infrastructure across France, but chronic 4-player price competition (Free/Iliad, SFR, Bouygues) and Spanish low-cost pressure compress 5-year ROIC to ~4% (far below 12% hurdle) and eliminate pricing power.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (gate_3b_pricing_and_proof = 'N', REJECT). Sub-hurdle historical returns on capital (5-year ROIC of 3.6-5.2%, well below the 12% threshold) and chronic four-carrier price wars in France (Free, SFR, Bouygues) and Spain eliminate pricing power >= inflation.
column21: Orange operates extensive telecom infrastructure in France, Europe, and MEA. However, capital intensity is massive and 5-year average ROIC is ~4.3% (trailing WACC). French low-cost competition and Spanish promotional pressure prevent real pricing power and sub-hurdle capital returns violate Gate 3b.

column14: Dominant Swiss telecom infrastructure generates steady domestic cash flow, but Swiss revenue is stagnant/deflationary and the debt-funded €8B acquisition of Vodafone Italia dilutes ROIC to ~10.9% with sub-8% incremental ROIIC in a competitive Italian telecom market.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (gate_3b_pricing_and_proof = 'N', REJECT). Core Swiss telecom revenue has been stagnant-to-deflationary for years, and the €8B debt-financed acquisition of Vodafone Italia dilutes ROIC to ~10.9% with incremental ROIIC well below the 12% hurdle in a brutally competitive Italian market.
column21: Swisscom maintains dominant market shares in Switzerland with 13% median historical ROIC. However, domestic revenue grew 0% over 2022-2024. The 100% debt-funded acquisition of Vodafone Italia (€8B) increases net debt-to-EBITDA to ~2.7x and generates sub-8% incremental ROIIC, diluting 2025 GAAP ROIC to 10.94% and failing Gate 3b proof of moat.

column14: Challenger telecom operator in Switzerland (#2 behind Swisscom); relies heavily on promotional discounts and Yallo discount sub-brand to defend market share; coax broadband base faces steady FTTH migration losses, yielding sub-10% ROIC and zero real pricing power.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (gate_3b_pricing_and_proof = 'N', REJECT). Swiss #2 challenger relies on aggressive discounting and its Yallo sub-brand to retain subscribers against Swisscom and Salt, generating sub-10% ROIC and flat-to-declining real ARPU with no pricing power.
column21: Spun off from Liberty Global in late 2024, Sunrise operates mobile and hybrid-fiber-coax (HFC) networks in Switzerland. It carries high leverage (3.5x-4.5x EBITDA, BB- credit rating) while facing continuous customer losses on coax to Swisscom/utility fiber networks. Lack of pricing power and sub-10% ROIC fail Gate 3b.

column14: Incumbent telecom networks and spectrum across Spain, Brazil, and Germany, but hyper-competition from low-cost challengers (e.g. Digi in Spain) and heavy spectrum/fiber capex keep 5-year ROIC depressed at 3-4% (well below the 12% hurdle) with zero real pricing power.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (gate_3b_pricing_and_proof = 'N', REJECT). Chronic 5-year ROIC of 3-4% falls far short of the 12% threshold. Intense low-cost competition in Spain (Digi, MasOrange) eliminates pricing power >= inflation, while €25B+ net debt burden reflects decades of value-dilutive empire building.
column21: Telefónica is the Spanish incumbent telecom operator with major operations in Spain, Brazil, and Germany. Heavy ongoing capital intensity and relentless price competition have depressed 5-year ROIC to ~3.5-4.0%. Massive net debt (€25.3B financial debt, ~€33B including leases) and repeated dividend cuts fail Gate 3b proof of moat.

column14: National mobile towers and fixed fiber infrastructure provide a durable physical asset base, but stringent wholesale open-access regulation in Norway and aggressive Nordic retail price competition keep 5-year ROIC chronically sub-hurdle (~8-10%) with real ARPU lagging inflation.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC ~8-10% < 12%, sub-inflation pricing power, REJECT). State-backed Nordic telecom incumbent owns critical physical network assets, but heavy ongoing 5G/fiber capex, strict Norwegian wholesale open-access regulation, and intense retail competition prevent earning excess economic returns on capital.
column21: Reported ROCE has hovered between 8.9% and 11.5% over 2020-2024, with GAAP ROIC averaging ~8-10%, failing the 12% threshold. Significant leverage (>NOK 100B net debt including lease liabilities; net debt to EBITDA ~2.2x). Restructuring of Asian holdings (True Corp JV in Thailand, CelcomDigi in Malaysia) has resulted in historical write-downs without lifting core Nordic capital returns.

column14: Strong cash generation in the Baltic mobile oligopoly is diluted by the larger Swedish market, where intense competition against Telia, Telenor, and 3 constrains pricing power below inflation and keeps multi-year ROIC (~8-10%) below the 12% cost-of-capital threshold.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC ~8-10% < 12%, pricing power below inflation, REJECT). While Tele2 operates a lean telecom challenger model with strong Baltic cash generation and Iliad backing, Swedish mobile and broadband competition restricts real pricing power and keeps multi-cycle capital returns below the 12% hurdle.
column21: Reported ROCE was 8% in 2021, 11% in 2022 (inflated by Netherlands divestment gain), 10% in 2023, and 11% in 2024, with multi-year GAAP ROIC running at 8-10%, failing Gate 3b. Net debt to EBITDA remains ~2.3-2.5x with substantial ongoing 5G network capex required to maintain competitive parity.

column14: Incumbent Nordic network infrastructure and spectrum holdings are unreplicable, but wholesale open-access obligations and intense retail competition prevent earning excess returns, resulting in chronic 4-6% ROIC and real pricing erosion.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC 4-6% << 12%, negative real pricing power, REJECT). Swedish telecom incumbent suffers from chronic sub-hurdle capital returns, value-destructive media acquisitions (Bonnier Broadcasting/TV4), and inability to price above inflation amidst heavy 5G/fiber capital expenditure.
column21: Reported ROCE has languished between 4.8% and 6.9% across 2021-2024, with GAAP ROIC averaging ~4-6%, well below the 12% hurdle. High leverage with net debt/EBITDA >2.4x and repeated restructuring charges. Free cash flow generation is heavily absorbed by dividend commitments and infrastructure reinvestment.

column11: Listing country outside approved Western developed markets (in_market == N); discretionary hit-driven video game entertainment with multi-year gaps between releases.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (in_market == N and discretionary hit-driven entertainment, REJECT). Primary listing in Poland is outside the approved rule-of-law Western developed market tier. Furthermore, AAA video game development (The Witcher, Cyberpunk 2077) is inherently lumpy, hit-driven discretionary entertainment with multi-year dry spells between releases, lacking non-discretionary everyday demand.
column21: Poland is designated in_market == N. Financially, earnings and cash flows are hyper-cyclical, swinging violently depending on AAA game launches (e.g. massive revenue spike upon Cyberpunk 2077 launch followed by multi-year release lulls). Lacks recurring everyday subscription cash flows.

column14: Unassailable UK automotive marketplace toll booth with overwhelming two-sided network effects (>75% UK consumer automotive engagement time). UK car dealers cannot operate without listing inventory on Auto Trader. Proven pricing power with consistent mid-single-digit ARPA expansion exceeding inflation and ~65-70% operating margins. Low threat of erosion from horizontal classifieds or US entrants.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Dominant UK automotive marketplace toll booth with overwhelming two-sided network effects and indispensable dealer forecourt integration. Proven pricing power with consistent ARPA expansion and ~65-70% operating margins. Balance sheet fortress with net debt repayable in six months. [5-10Y g: dealer forecourt stock 0.5% + core ARPA price tiering 4.5% + Deal Builder product mix 1.0% - cloud/tech reinvestment 0.5% + net share repurchases 2.5%]
column21: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 48.4% with operating ROIC >100%. Free cash flow conversion exceeds 100% of Net Income (£290.2M Owner FCF in FY25). Operating profit margin consistently ~63-70%. Interest coverage exceeds 80x with net debt/EBITDA <0.4x. Steady share buybacks reducing share count.

column14: Dominant German real estate marketplace toll booth (ImmoScout24) with self-reinforcing two-sided network effects. High customer switching costs from deep agent CRM integration and tenant MieterPlus/SCHUFA verification lock-in. Demonstrated exceptional pricing power by compounding revenue and ARPU ahead of inflation throughout the severe 2022-2025 German property freeze, sustaining ~44-48% operating margins and >100% tangible operating ROIC.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Undisputed German real estate marketplace toll booth (ImmoScout24) with dual-sided agent and tenant-subscription lock-in that expanded ARPU and earnings even through Germany's residential property downturn. Debt-free balance sheet with >100% FCF conversion. [5-10Y g: agent/tenant subscriber volume 2.0% + core listing price 3.5% + digital workflow product mix 1.5% - IT/cloud reinvestment 0.5% + net share repurchases 2.0%]
column21: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 12.7% with tangible operating ROIC >100%. Free cash flow conversion exceeds 100% of Net Income (€262.8M Owner FCF in FY25). Operating profit margin ~44-48% (EBITDA margin >55%). Zero long-term financial debt, net cash position, and interest coverage >70x. Consistent share repurchases and growing dividends.

column11: Core economic value and look-through earnings reside predominantly in non-Western jurisdictions (China VIE stake in Tencent, India, Brazil) lacking Western rule of law and property rights.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Prosus is an investment holding company whose asset value and look-through earnings are overwhelmingly concentrated in non-Western emerging markets (specifically Tencent in China via offshore VIE structures, Swiggy in India, and iFood in Brazil) lacking rule-of-law Western property rights.
column21: Over 70% of Prosus NAV and equity-accounted earnings stem from Tencent Holdings in China. Consolidated operating FCF conversion is extremely low (~8% of GAAP net income) due to non-cash associate earnings. Capital allocation history outside Tencent includes catastrophic capital destruction (e.g., 100% write-off of $500M+ Byju's investment, $1.8B acquisition of Stack Overflow).

column14: Unmatched two-sided network effects create an indispensable toll booth for UK estate agents and home movers (>80% consumer portal time share). Demonstrated pricing power through unbroken multi-year ARPA expansion across housing cycles with operating margins ~70% and agency retention >90%.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Dominant UK property portal operating an indispensable two-sided network toll booth with >80% consumer attention share. Demonstrated pricing power through steady ARPA increases above inflation across housing cycles, ~70% operating margins, and a net-cash fortress balance sheet. [5-10Y g: agency branch count 0.0% + ARPA pricing/upsell 4.5% + new products (mortgages/commercial) 1.0% - defensive tech/marketing spend 0.5% + net share buybacks 2.5%]
column21: Multi-year GAAP ROIC >100% on minimal invested capital. Operating margins steady around 68-70%. FCF conversion is ~100% (£219.4M Owner FCF on £217.1M Net Income in FY25). Fortress net cash balance sheet with £37.1M cash against £3.6M debt (EBIT interest coverage >2800x). Rejected opportunistic takeover approaches from REA Group at ~£6.2B, confirming standalone franchise durability.

column14: While FINN.no maintains strong localized classified network effects in Norway, the consolidated group fails the empirical proof-of-moat hurdle with a 5-year median GAAP ROIC of only 2.5%, sub-15% tangible ROIC, and negative operating income in FY25 (-NOK 166M).
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Consolidated entity fails the empirical proof-of-moat hurdle with a 5-year median GAAP ROIC of only 2.5% (and FY25 EBIT of -NOK 166M). Erratic capital efficiency, complex corporate reorganizations, and negative operating margins post-Schibsted demerger fail to demonstrate sustained group-wide pricing power.
column21: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 2.5% (0.0246) and tangible ROIC median is ~3.4%, far below the 12%/15% hurdles. FY25 EBIT was -NOK 166M with net income of -NOK 184M. Multi-year corporate restructuring following the news media demerger to Tinius Trust and the Adevinta private equity buyout has produced severe earnings volatility and depressed consolidated returns on capital.

column11: Live concerts and stadium entertainment are discretionary leisure activities deferrable in economic downturns, and booking fee take-rates face persistent regulatory and consumer antitrust scrutiny.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Live concerts, festival tours, and arena events are discretionary leisure activities easily deferred during economic downturns. In addition, Eventim's ticketing toll-booth fees and exclusive promoter/venue tie-ups face escalating regulatory and antitrust scrutiny across Europe.
column21: CTS Eventim is Europe's leading ticketing platform and live entertainment promoter. However, live event attendance is entirely discretionary entertainment that experienced severe impairment during economic lockdowns. Ticketing operations face constant regulatory scrutiny over booking fees and dynamic pricing from European competition authorities.

column11: Recorded music and music publishing represent discretionary media consumption rather than an essential functional necessity or entrenched non-deferrable household staple.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Recorded music and publishing are discretionary entertainment media rather than essential functional necessities or non-deferrable daily rituals. UMG operates primarily as an upstream wholesale licensor to downstream streaming DSPs without direct consumer pricing power.
column21: UMG owns leading recorded music and publishing catalogues (Taylor Swift, Drake, The Beatles). While music consumption is ubiquitous, it is discretionary leisure. UMG relies on downstream DSP distributors (Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube) for monetization, exposing it to platform negotiation pressure and royalty pool dilution from AI-generated audio.

column14: Must-attend B2B exhibitions (World of Concrete, Arab Health) and high-impact academic journal subscriptions (Taylor & Francis) demonstrate steady 3-5% annual pricing power above inflation; tangible ROIC >15%.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (Rejected – G6 Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet). Informa's aggressive serial M&A rollup strategy (UBM, Ascential) has loaded the balance sheet with £2.7B+ in long-term debt and £10.4B in goodwill/intangibles, depressing FY25 interest coverage to an unsafe 0.6x (EBIT £94.6M vs interest £158.9M) and failing the peace-of-mind solvency standard.
column21: While Informa owns premier event franchises and Taylor & Francis journals, multi-year GAAP ROIC has been depressed to a 4.3% median by serial M&A. In FY25, reported net income plummeted to £11M and EBIT dropped to £94.6M against £158.9M in interest expense (0.6x coverage). Long-term debt of £2,727.6M exceeds 4x normalized net income, failing Gate 6 balance sheet criteria.

column11: 100% of operations and revenues are concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa (14 African nations) outside Western developed rule-of-law markets, exposed to severe currency devaluations and sovereign regulatory extraction.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Essential Western Need). While providing essential telecom and mobile money services across 14 Sub-Saharan African countries, 100% of operations and revenue originate outside Western developed markets, suffering severe structural currency devaluations (e.g. Nigerian Naira) and high sovereign/regulatory risks.
column21: Airtel Africa operates across Nigeria, East Africa, and Francophone Africa. Severe FX devaluations (e.g. Nigerian Naira collapse in FY24) have repeatedly crushed USD/GBP reported profits and cash conversion despite local currency growth. Revenue base concentrated entirely in non-Western emerging markets violates Gate 2.

column14: Operates as a network-independent reseller (MVNO) dependent on wholesale access contracts from Deutsche Telekom, Vodafone, and Telefónica Deutschland, alongside an IPTV service (waipu.tv). Lacks pricing power in commoditized mobile plans, resulting in 5-year median GAAP ROIC below the 12% threshold.
column20: Fails Gate 3 (Moat & Pricing Power). Operates as a mobile reseller (MVNO) without own network infrastructure and IPTV provider (waipu.tv). Sub-hurdle historical capital efficiency (5-year median GAAP ROIC ~8-10% vs 12% threshold) and negligible pricing power amid aggressive discount mobile competition.
column21: freenet acts as a service provider dependent on network operator wholesale agreements. Multi-year GAAP ROIC hovers around 8-10%, failing the 12% hurdle. German mobile tariff competition severely limits standalone price hikes, forcing reliance on SG&A discipline and high dividend payouts rather than economic moat expansion.

column14: Possesses extensive European spectrum and fixed cable network assets, but operates in structurally commoditized, capital-intensive markets. Chronic value destruction is evidenced by 5-year GAAP ROIC languishing between 0.1% and 3.8% (well below 12% threshold) and inability to price above inflation.
column20: Fails Gate 3 (Moat & Pricing Power). Capital-intensive telecom network operator across Europe and Africa. Suffers from chronic sub-hurdle capital efficiency (5-year GAAP ROIC <4% vs 12% hurdle), heavy recurring 5G/cable capex, and lack of pricing power amid cutthroat market competition and regulatory price scrutiny.
column21: Vodafone's multi-year ROIC has persistently trailed WACC, averaging <4% for over a decade. Elevated debt (>€30B) prompted distressed divestments of Italian and Spanish units. In Germany (largest market), the abolition of the housing association bulk-billing privilege (Nebenkostenprivileg) in 2024 sparked severe TV subscriber losses. Structural failure of Gate 3b.

column14: Operates Vodafone Spain (acquired May 2024 via €5B debt-heavy buyout). Faces intense price deflation and churn in the Spanish telecom market from aggressive low-cost competitors (Digi Spain) and scale incumbents (Telefónica, MasOrange). Lacks pricing power >= inflation, with historical ROIC well below the 12% threshold.
column20: Fails Gate 3 (Moat & Pricing Power). Highly leveraged buyout vehicle operating Vodafone Spain. Spain is one of Europe's most commoditized, price-deflationary telecom markets where ultra-low-cost disruptors (Digi) preclude pricing power >= inflation, resulting in sub-hurdle historical ROIC (<12%).
column21: Zegona acquired Vodafone Spain in 2024 for €5B financed with heavy debt (€3.2B+ net debt, ~2.3-3.1x EBITDAaL). Historical ROIC under Vodafone and post-acquisition is negative to low single-digit, failing the 12% hurdle. The Spanish market suffers from relentless promotional discounting and lack of pricing power.

column11: Discretionary fast-fashion apparel; purchases are deferrable and non-essential during economic downturns, highly vulnerable to fashion cycle shifts and low-cost substitution.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Essential Western Need). Fast-fashion apparel is discretionary, deferrable, and easily forgone during economic downturns. H&M lacks Lindy brand equity or mission-critical utility, facing severe competitive substitution from ultra-fast-fashion platforms (Shein, Temu) and agile near-sourced peers (Zara).
column21: H&M operates over 4,000 stores globally in fast fashion. When inflation and cost-of-living pressures squeezed European consumers in 2022-2024, sales stalled and operating margins compressed to 6-8%, requiring heavy promotional markdowns to clear seasonal inventory. Discretionary, trend-driven fashion fails Gate 2.

column14: Proprietary proximity sourcing (Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Turkey) and store-level real-time data feedback loops allow 2-3 week concept-to-rack turnaround. Generates elite 58-61% gross margins and 35-45% GAAP ROIC, virtually eliminating inventory markdown obsolescence.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global apparel retail leader powered by proprietary proximity-sourcing supply chain and real-time inventory optimization. Exceptional capital efficiency with 40%+ ROIC and €10B+ net cash fortress balance sheet. [5-10Y g: store/online volume 3.5% + price/mix 2.0% + floor-space optimization 1.0% - logistics wage drag 0.5% + dividend/cash return 1.0%]
column21: Multi-cycle GAAP ROIC exceeding 35-45%, gross margins stable at 58-61%, and operating margins ~20%. Proximity sourcing (Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Turkey) and automated distribution allow 2-3 week cycle times, virtually eliminating markdown risk. Inditex carries over €10B in net cash with multi-year FCF conversion near 100%.

column11: Listing country Poland is outside approved rule-of-law Western markets (in_market == N); fast fashion retail is non-essential, fashion-cycle dependent, and easily forgone in downturns.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Primary listing in Poland is outside approved rule-of-law Western markets (in_market == N). Fast-fashion and value apparel retail (Reserved, Sinsay) is highly discretionary, cyclical, and easily forgone during economic downturns.
column21: LPP S.A. operates over 2,200 stores across 27+ countries with brands including Reserved, Sinsay, Cropp, House, and Mohito. The business is heavily exposed to Central & Eastern European consumer purchasing power and currency volatility (PLN). Fast-fashion apparel faces intense competition from global peers (Inditex/Zara, H&M, Shein) with low customer switching costs. The company faced severe governance scrutiny following short-seller allegations regarding post-2022 Russia asset divestment. Poland is classified as in_market == N in the screener universe.

column14: Global athletic brand heritage and multi-decade sports sponsorship scale. Gross margins consistently remain around ~50% across cycles, though operating profitability fluctuates with footwear fashion trends and inventory clearing.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). Athletic footwear and apparel face severe fashion-trend cycle risks, hit-franchise saturation (Samba/Gazelle fatigue), and intense market share erosion from agile challenger brands (On, Hoka). High Asian contract manufacturing exposure introduces persistent supply chain and tariff vulnerabilities.
column21: Adidas generates over €21B in revenue across footwear (~50%+), apparel, and accessories. While gross margins have recovered to ~51% under CEO Bjørn Gulden following the termination of the Yeezy partnership, historical GAAP ROIC has been volatile (17.6% in 2019, 4.0% in 2022, -2.1% in 2023, recovering to ~8.5% in 2024). The business model is repeatedly subject to hit-franchise overproduction cycles (Stan Smith, Superstar, Boost, Yeezy, Samba) followed by promotional discounting. Supply chain is heavily dependent on outsourced factories in Vietnam, Indonesia, and China.

column11: High-end luxury apparel and ready-to-wear cashmere are discretionary, cyclical fashion purchases easily forgone during economic downturns.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Ultra-luxury ready-to-wear cashmere and designer apparel represent discretionary, fashion-sensitive purchases easily forgone in economic downturns. Does not possess the multi-generational Lindy permanence of hard luxury or iconic leather goods.
column21: Brunello Cucinelli SpA produces ultra-luxury apparel and lifestyle goods rooted in Solomeo, Italy. While the company maintains disciplined full-price retail distribution and gross margins above 65%, its revenue is predominantly concentrated in ready-to-wear seasonal apparel. Multi-year GAAP ROIC has ranged between 7% and 12%, failing to consistently clear the 12% hurdle. The company faced scrutiny in 2025 regarding Russian market sales. Discretionary high-ticket clothing lacks the non-deferrable utility or Lindy moat required under Munger screening criteria.

column11: Discretionary aspirational luxury fashion and trench apparel easily forgone or delayed during cyclical economic downturns.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Discretionary aspirational luxury outerwear and seasonal fashion apparel are easily forgone during economic contractions. The brand suffers from repeated strategic repositionings between upmarket elevation and discounting, lacking pricing power.
column21: Burberry Group plc has suffered severe strategic and financial turbulence. Under successive leadership changes (Marco Gobbetti, Jonathan Akeroyd, Joshua Schulman) and creative directors (Riccardo Tisci, Daniel Lee), the brand attempted to push aggressively upmarket with steep price increases, alienating aspirational buyers without winning ultra-high-net-worth loyalty. FY2025 adjusted operating profit collapsed from £418M (14.1% margin) in FY24 to just £26M (1.0% margin), group ROIC turned negative, and the dividend was suspended. The company executed pro-cyclical share repurchases at valuation peaks before suspending payouts to preserve liquidity.

column14: Unrivaled branded jewellery duopoly (Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels) supported by centuries of Lindy heritage and protected designs (Love, Trinity, Alhambra). Pricing power proven by 4-8% regular annual price hikes with zero volume churn, generating 17-21% multi-cycle ROIC.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Premier hard luxury and branded jewellery duopoly (Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels) possessing centuries-old Lindy heritage and unmatched pricing power. YNAP divestment cleanly prunes the e-commerce drag, refocusing capital on high-ROIC Jewellery Maisons. Balance sheet fortress with over €8.2B in net cash. [5-10Y g: branded jewellery volume 3.5% + luxury pricing power 3.5% + retail expansion mix 1.0% - watch cycle drag 0.5% + dividends/buybacks 1.0%]
column21: Compagnie Financière Richemont SA generates ~€20B+ in revenue, with Jewellery Maisons (Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels, Buccellati) accounting for ~70% of sales and ~85% of operating profit at 30%+ operating margins. Operating ROIC has averaged 17-21% over the past four years (FY22: 15.4%, FY23: 21.1%, FY24: 19.4%, FY25: 17.7%). Net cash stood at €8.26B at FY2025 year-end with zero net debt. Branded fine jewellery benefits from a secular mix shift away from unbranded items, with Cartier and VCA wielding pricing power to raise prices 4-8% annually above inflation without sacrificing volume.

column11: Discretionary fashion luxury and leather goods heavily dependent on trend cycles (Gucci), easily forgone and deferred in downturns.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Discretionary fashion apparel and trend-driven leather goods (Gucci over-reliance) are non-essential and easily forgone during economic downturns. The brand lacks the multi-generational Lindy pricing power of Hermès or Cartier, suffering severe volume contraction when fashion trends shift.
column21: Kering SA has suffered severe earnings contraction due to Gucci's brand fatigue and fashion cycle unwinding. Recurring operating income plunged from €4.75B in 2023 to €2.44B in 2024 and €1.63B in 2025. ROIC fell from ~16% (2022) to ~11% (2023) and ~3.4-5% in 2024-2025. Unlike secular luxury compounders, Kering carried €8.0B to €10.5B in net debt following debt-funded acquisitions (Creed for ~€3.5B, 30% of Valentino, and prime real estate purchases at cycle peaks), leading S&P to downgrade its credit rating to BBB+. The business model is highly cyclical, discretionary, and fashion-trend sensitive.

column14: Portfolio of 75 irreplaceable heritage maisons (Louis Vuitton, Dior, Tiffany, Sephora, Moët Hennessy) backed by centuries of brand equity, prime global flagship real estate, and exclusive viticulture terroir. Scale allows dominant marketing spend and prime retail access that challengers cannot match. Proved by 22-26% recurring operating margins and >20% tangible operating ROIC across cycles. Primary erosion threats include aspirational brand overexposure, Chinese consumer slowdown, and cyclical downturns in cognac/champagne.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global titan of luxury goods with 75 heritage maisons led by Louis Vuitton, Dior, and Sephora. Enduring pricing power, prime global retail real estate, and irreplaceable terroir protect superior returns. Fortress balance sheet with net debt under 0.5x EBITDA. [5-10Y g: luxury volume 3.5% + pricing power 2.5% + retail expansion/mix 1.5% - marketing reinvestment drag 0.5% + share repurchases 0.5%]
column21: FY2025 revenue of €80.8B and recurring operating profit of €17.8B (22.0% margin). 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~12.5% with tangible operating ROIC >20%. Net financial debt reduced to €6.9B, repayable in under 1 year of net income. Interest coverage exceeds 15x. Arnault family holds ~64% voting control ensuring long-term stewardship.

column14: High-end brand prestige, alpine heritage, and controlled direct-to-consumer store network (~80%+ DTC) protect >29% operating margins and ROIC >20%. Strong pricing power in technical down jackets. Primary erosion threats include fashion fatigue, warming winter climates, narrow category concentration, and heavy dependence on Chinese consumer spending.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). Premium luxury outerwear brand with outstanding margins (~29% EBIT) and pristine net cash (>€1.4B), but structurally constrained by single-category seasonal product concentration (down jackets). Lacks the multi-category Lindy durability of century-old luxury houses and faces long-term headwinds from fashion cycle shifts and warming winter climates.
column21: FY2025 revenue of €3,132M and EBIT of €913M (29.2% margin) with net cash of €1.46B. Despite exceptional current profitability and >20% ROIC, Moncler brand generates >85% of group revenue, heavily skewed toward winter outerwear and Chinese luxury consumers (~50% Asia revenue). Narrow product category and fashion-trend sensitivity restrict 15+ year competitive advantage runway.

column11: Discretionary affordable fashion jewellery; non-essential gift purchase easily forgone or deferred during economic downturns.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). Accessible and affordable fashion jewellery is entirely discretionary and easily forgone during economic downturns. Charms and silver jewelry lack essential need status, Lindy durability, or the inelastic pricing power of true ultra-luxury houses, while remaining heavily exposed to volatile precious metal input costs.
column21: World's largest jewellery maker by volume, operating high-volume manufacturing facilities in Thailand and Vietnam. Despite strong recent execution, the core product offering remains anchored in discretionary silver charm bracelets where silver represents ~30% of COGS. Operating in the accessible fashion jewellery tier exposes the business to middle-income consumer spending pullbacks and fashion fad risk.

column11: Discretionary sportswear and footwear; non-essential fashion brand lacking entrenched everyday habit and easily substituted.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). Sportswear and athletic sneakers are discretionary fashion items easily deferred or substituted. Puma lacks an entrenched everyday habit, proprietary moat, or pricing power, suffering from brand dilution through promotional off-price wholesale channels and severe margin compression during industry inventory resets.
column21: FY2025 sales declined 8.1% currency-adjusted to €7,296M while reported EBIT plunged to -€357M (adjusted EBIT -€166M) due to promotional wholesale discounting and 1,400 corporate headcount cuts. Puma lacks pricing power against dominant players (Nike, Adidas) and nimble innovators (On, Hoka), leaving it exposed to violent retail wholesale destocking cycles.

column14: Artisan capacity bottlenecks, multi-year waitlists for iconic Birkin and Kelly bags, and multi-generational French leathercrafting heritage create an unreplicable luxury moat. Returns protected by refusing volume growth beyond artisan training capacity (~7% annual volume cap). Proved by 70%+ GAAP ROIC and >40% recurring operating margins through all macro cycles. Primary erosion risks are counterfeit proliferation and potential over-commercialization of non-leather categories.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Quintessential ultra-luxury scarcity maison with unmatched brand prestige and pricing power. Birkin and Kelly waitlists and artisan capacity limits preserve scarcity and >40% EBIT margins. Fortress balance sheet with >€12B net cash. [5-10Y g: artisan volume 6.0% + pricing power 3.5% + product mix 1.0% - tax/capex drag 0.5% + share repurchases 0.0%]
column21: FY2025 revenue reached €16,002M (+9% cFX) with recurring operating margin of 41.0% (€6,569M). 5-year GAAP ROIC exceeds 70% (median 96%). Balance sheet holds €12,239M in cash against only €34M long-term debt, yielding over €12B in net cash. Owner FCF conversion exceeds 90% (€4.3B FCF in FY25). Family-controlled ownership structure ensures multi-generational discipline.

column11: Discretionary wristwatches; non-essential accessories easily forgone and substituted by smart devices during cyclical downturns.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). Traditional quartz and mechanical wristwatches are non-essential discretionary accessories easily deferred during downturns and structurally challenged by smart wearables. Massive unabsorbed fixed manufacturing capacity and heavy exposure to volatile Chinese retail demand produce severe cyclical earnings collapses.
column21: FY2025 net sales fell to CHF 6,280M with Group operating margin collapsing to 2.1% (CHF 135M EBIT) and net income of just CHF 25M, down from CHF 1,191M operating profit in 2023. Management's refusal to adjust production capacity in its industrial manufacturing segment (ETA/components) through severe Chinese demand contractions destroys capital returns (ROIC < 2%).

column14: Premium brand equity ('Ultimate Driving Machine') and flexible multi-powertrain manufacturing across BMW, Mini, and Rolls-Royce provide moderate brand loyalty. However, capital efficiency is structurally cyclical and sub-hurdle, with Automotive RoCE falling to 6.6% in 2024 and Group ROIC averaging 7-9% across the cycle (well below the 12% hurdle). Primary erosion threats include aggressive Chinese EV competition (especially in China, ~30% of volume), regulatory fleet emissions mandates, software-defined vehicle execution risks, and customer cross-shopping price elasticity.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & pricing power, REJECT). Premium automotive manufacturing is structurally capital-intensive and cyclical, with Automotive RoCE dropping from a 24% peak in 2021 to 6.6% in 2024 (multi-cycle Group ROIC 7-9% vs 12% hurdle). Faces aggressive Chinese EV price competition, heavy Neue Klasse capex/R&D burdens, and customer cross-shopping elasticity.
column21: Automotive segment RoCE dropped from 24.0% in 2021 and 18.1% in 2022 to 11.3% in 2023 and 6.6% in 2024. Group ROIC over full business cycles hovers around 7-9%, failing the 12% hurdle. Massive ongoing R&D and capex for Neue Klasse electric architecture and software platforms depress returns on incremental capital. China sales (~30% of deliveries) suffer from intense local EV price wars, and vehicle recall disruptions (such as the Continental integrated braking system in 2024) illustrate vulnerability in outsourced critical component supply chains.

column14: Three-pointed star brand equity, premier engineering heritage, and commercial van dominance (Sprinter) provide brand premium over volume OEMs. However, pricing power has proven cyclical rather than structural, as top-end luxury EV push (EQS/EQE) met customer resistance and Chinese luxury buyers rotated to domestic tech-forward EV offerings. Group ROCE declined to 6.8% in 2024 (multi-cycle average 8-10%, failing the 12% hurdle). Key threats: China volume/pricing collapse, EV transition friction, and unionized manufacturing cost structures.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & pricing power, REJECT). Mercedes-Benz's 'top-end luxury' strategy failed to establish durable pricing power beyond the post-pandemic supply constraint windfall. Group ROCE declined to 6.8% in 2024 (multi-cycle ROCE 8-10% vs 12% hurdle), with cars division RoS compressing to 8-10%. High German manufacturing cost structure, heavy EV capex, and severe market share losses to Chinese luxury EVs in Asia erode economic returns.
column21: Group ROCE contracted from 10.1% in 2022 to 10.0% in 2023 and 6.8% in 2024. Adjusted Return on Sales (RoS) for Mercedes-Benz Cars dropped from 14.6% in 2022 to ~8-10% in 2024. Multi-cycle ROIC averages below 9%, failing the 12% hurdle. In China, which accounted for over a third of high-margin S-Class and Maybach sales, local EV competition and macroeconomic softening triggered deep discounting. Heavy dual capex/R&D spending across internal combustion, hybrid, and battery-electric architectures restricts incremental capital returns.

column11: Discretionary big-ticket purchase deferrable in recessions; luxury sports cars and performance SUVs represent non-essential, postponable purchases.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (discretionary big-ticket deferrable cyclical, REJECT). Luxury sports cars and high-performance SUVs (Macan, Cayenne, 911, Taycan) represent postponable big-ticket purchases rather than essential functional necessities or high-frequency everyday rituals. Sales collapsed in China (-30%+) and Group RoS compressed from 18% to 14% as discretionary demand softened.
column21: Porsche produces over 300,000 vehicles annually, with the vast majority comprised of Macan and Cayenne SUVs rather than scarce collector sports cars. In 2024, group operating profit dropped from €7.28B to €5.64B and Return on Sales contracted from 18.0% to 14.1%, driven by a severe ~30% volume slump in China, delays and customer friction in EV transitions (Taycan/Macan EV), and dealer discounting. Governance remains entangled with Volkswagen Group and Porsche Automobil Holding SE.

column14: Deliberate scarcity model and Formula 1 heritage volume automakers cannot copy without self-cannibalization. Proof of moat: 25%+ ROIC across economic cycles, ~50% gross margins, 38%+ EBITDA margins, and a 2+ year sold-out order backlog. Extreme pricing power demonstrated by personalization options contributing over 19% of revenues. Key erosion threats include brand dilution if volume expands beyond luxury scarcity limits, powertrain sound/emotional shift in the transition to hybrid/EVs, and European small-volume emissions derogation changes.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (FCF conversion < 80%, REJECT). Despite possessing one of the world's most formidable luxury moats (30Y CAP, 25%+ ROIC, multi-year order backlogs), Ferrari fails Pillar 2 FCF conversion: 5-year cumulative Industrial FCF / Net Income is ~68.4% (67.3% in 2024, 74.1% in 2023), missing the strict 80% cash conversion threshold due to continuous heavy automotive manufacturing capex and capitalized development outlays for new model architectures.
column21: Ferrari generated €1,526M net income and €1,027M industrial FCF in 2024 (67.3% conversion), and €1,257M net income and €932M industrial FCF in 2023 (74.1% conversion). Cumulative 2020-2024 industrial FCF of €3,531M against net income of €5,164M yields 68.4% conversion, failing the Gate 6 80% threshold. Operating ROIC exceeds 25%, gross margins exceed 49%, and order books are fully committed through 2026. Consolidated gross debt stands at €3.35B (including €1.66B financial services debt) against €3.53B equity and €1.74B cash.

column14: Dacia brand design-to-cost engineering provides a genuine low-cost value proposition in entry-level European passenger cars. However, mass-market volume automotive manufacturing is fundamentally commoditized and capital-intensive. Multi-cycle Group ROIC has averaged ~2-3% (well below the 12% hurdle), with operating margins structurally constrained between 3% and 8%. Primary erosion threats: low-cost Chinese EV imports into Europe, stringent EU fleet emissions penalties, cyclical consumer demand, and execution complexity across its unbundled Horse (ICE) and Ampere (EV) divisions.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & pricing power, REJECT). Despite Dacia's low-cost design-to-cost discipline under the 'Renaulution' turnaround, Renault operates in the structurally commoditized European volume auto market. Multi-cycle Group ROIC averages just 2-3% (far below the 12% hurdle), with operating margins capped around 7-8%. Severe price competition from low-cost Chinese EV entrants and heavy powertrain transition capex destroy excess returns.
column21: Consolidated Group ROIC hovered between 0.9% and 3.0% from 2021 to 2024, failing the 12% hurdle across the cycle. Group operating margins stabilized at 7.6% in 2024 (€4.26B operating income on €56.2B revenue), but remain vulnerable to cyclical downshifts. High structural capital expenditures required for the EV transition, cancellation of the Ampere IPO, complex cross-shareholdings with Nissan, and intense pricing pressure from imported Chinese EVs in Europe prevent the generation of durable economic rents.

column14: Merger scale across 14 legacy brands (PSA and FCA) provided temporary platform synergies and cost rationalization. However, Stellantis lacks structural pricing power: excessive post-pandemic price hikes alienated US dealers and customers, resulting in massive market share losses, a costly inventory glut, and a collapse in Adjusted Operating Income margin to 5.5% with -€6.0B industrial FCF in 2024. Primary erosion threats: severe brand fragmentation, Chinese EV competition in Europe, union labor conflicts in the US (UAW) and Europe, and leadership vacuum following the departure of CEO Carlos Tavares.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% & pricing power, REJECT). Stellantis proved that its post-merger margins were cyclical windfall rather than structural pricing power. In 2024, AOI margin collapsed from 12.8% to 5.5%, industrial FCF plummeted to -€6.0B, and ROIC sank to 4.6%. Aggressive price hikes alienated dealers and consumers, triggering severe market share losses and an inventory crisis in North America that forced heavy discounting.
column21: In 2024, net revenues declined 17% to €156.9B, Adjusted Operating Income plunged 64% to €8.64B (5.5% margin vs 12.8% in 2023), and industrial free cash flow swung to negative €6.0B from +€12.9B in 2023. ROIC crashed from ~18% to ~4.6%. Aggressive pricing on Jeep and Ram trucks triggered a massive inventory buildup and dealer backlash in the US, forcing painful production cutbacks and price discounting. CEO Carlos Tavares resigned amidst operational turmoil, illustrating the lack of a durable competitive moat across 14 fragmented brands.

column14: Global volume scale and extensive dealer networks fail to protect economic returns. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~4.2%, far below the 12% threshold, burdened by high German union labor costs, massive capex/R&D requirements, and fierce price competition from Chinese EV entrants.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%, REJECT). Legacy automotive OEM burdened by structurally sub-hurdle capital efficiency (5-year median GAAP ROIC ~4.2%), high German union labor costs, software execution issues (CARIAD), and market share erosion in China against agile EV competitors.
column21: Automotive division ROI was 9.7% in 2024 and 10.4% in 2021, with group GAAP ROIC averaging ~3.5-4.2% over 5 years, well below the 12% hurdle. Massive capex and R&D requirements (~€20B+ annually) combined with aggressive EV price wars prevent economic profit generation.

column14: While the Tires division earns healthy ROCE (>20%), the consolidated Automotive and ContiTech divisions suffer from severe OEM buyer power and low profitability. 5-year median group GAAP ROIC/ROCE is ~7-8%, well below the 12% threshold.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%, REJECT). Consolidated group returns fail the 12% hurdle (5-year median ROCE ~7-8%) due to the low-margin Automotive supplier division (ROCE near breakeven) facing relentless pricing pressure from automotive OEMs, despite the high-quality Tires division.
column21: Group ROCE was 8.9% in 2021, 3.7% in 2022, 8.9% in 2023, and 11.4% in 2024. Automotive division ROCE languished at -0.6% in 2023 and 2.6% in 2024. Intense OEM buyer power and annual price-down mandates eliminate pricing power at or above inflation for the automotive segment.

column14: OEM qualification and engineering patents fail to yield economic rents. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 2.5-4.5%, deeply sub-hurdle, as powerful automotive OEMs demand continuous cost reductions and pass inflationary component costs back onto suppliers.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%, REJECT). Chronic capital inefficiency with 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 2.5-4.5%. Squeezed between concentrated OEM customer buyer power and high ongoing R&D/capex requirements for electrification and ADAS.
column21: Historical GAAP ROIC has persistently tracked between 2.5% and 4.5% across 2021-2024. Operating margins are thin (~3-4%), and operating cash flows are largely consumed by tangible capex and capitalized R&D to service OEM contracts.

column14: Commodity digital used-car merchant with no pricing power over market bid-ask spreads. Gross profit per unit is thin (~€1,000-€1,500), and historical 5-year GAAP ROIC has been negative due to continuous operating losses post-IPO.
column20: Fails Gate 3 (Moat Archetype None & ROIC < 12%, REJECT). Commodity used-car trading platform operating in a fragmented, highly competitive market with razor-thin gross profit margins per unit, working-capital and inventory financing intensity, and negative multi-year historical ROIC.
column21: Reported cumulative net losses from 2021 through 2023 (-€418M in 2021, -€275M in 2022, -€130M in 2023), reaching marginal net income (~€21M) only in 2024. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is negative. High inventory holding risk and reliance on asset-backed debt facilities.

column11: Discretionary travel-retail and airport luxury concessions easily forgone by travelers; captive airport landlords extract economic rents through concession fees.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Discretionary Travel Retail, REJECT). Airport duty-free shopping and concessions represent discretionary, non-essential impulse purchases that travelers readily forgo during economic slumps. Airport authorities act as monopoly landlords capturing surplus via concession tenders.
column21: Avolta (Dufry + Autogrill) relies on international airline passenger footfall. Concession agreements feature high minimum guaranteed fees (MAGs) paid to airport operators, while sales mix is heavily tilted toward deferrable duty-free luxury, cosmetics, alcohol, and tobacco.

column14: Belron's insurer integrations and global scale drive consistent price and mix gains above inflation, particularly from rising ADAS camera/sensor recalibration attach rates on replacement windshields.
column20: Fails Gate 6 (N, REJECT). While Belron (Carglass/Safelite) and TVH are exceptional, high-return operating assets, D'Ieteren fails Gate 6 due to massive leverage: late-2024 dividend recapitalizations saddled Belron with ~€9B in debt (rated BB-) to fund a €4B extraordinary dividend, driving D'Ieteren consolidated equity negative (-€457M in 2024) and look-through debt/Owner Earnings to ~8-10x.
column21: Consolidated balance sheet showed negative equity (-€456.9M) in FY2024 and thin equity (€14.3M) in FY2025 following the €74/share special dividend. Equity-accounted Belron incurred €3.8B in incremental debt, bringing net debt to ~€9B. Look-through debt/Owner Earnings exceeds the <=4.0x threshold by more than double.

column11: Listing country (Poland) is outside approved Western developed market universe (in_market = N); discretionary e-commerce marketplace facing intense cross-border platform competition.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (in_market = N, REJECT). Headquartered and listed in Poland, which falls outside the screener's approved Western developed market universe. Furthermore, discretionary e-commerce marketplace faces intense cross-border platform competition from Temu, Shein, and Amazon Poland, alongside past capital misallocation in the Mall Group acquisition.
column21: Allegro operates Poland's dominant online marketplace with >14 million active buyers and the Smart! loyalty subscription. However, Poland is excluded from the Western developed market list (in_market = N), triggering an automatic Gate 2 failure under screener rules. Economically, while domestic Polish GMV and EBITDA have been resilient, the cross-border acquisition of Mall Group resulted in a PLN 2.3B impairment in 2022, and long-term take-rates face persistent pricing pressure from Chinese cross-border discount platforms (Temu, Shein) and Amazon.

column11: Discretionary fashion and homeware apparel retail; non-essential consumer purchases easily deferred or traded down during economic downturns.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). Exceptional capital allocation under Simon Wolfson cannot overcome the fundamental nature of the product: discretionary fashion and homeware apparel, which is inherently deferrable in recessions and lacks customer lock-in.
column21: Next plc is an exceptionally well-managed UK omnichannel apparel retailer with ~£5B+ revenue, strong ROE/ROCE (>25%), and innovative logistics infrastructure via Total Platform. However, over 80% of earnings remain tethered to discretionary apparel, footwear, and home furnishings in the mature UK market. Consumer clothing purchases are non-essential, highly deferrable in inflationary or recessionary environments, and face intense long-term price competition from global fast-fashion players (Inditex, Shein, Primark).

column11: Discretionary fashion and footwear e-commerce; non-essential consumer purchases easily deferred during economic downturns amid intense competitive discounting.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). Online fashion and footwear retail is non-essential, discretionary, and deferrable. Structural industry headwinds include high return rates (up to 50%), brand disintermediation via direct-to-consumer channels, and fierce competition from ultra-fast-fashion platforms.
column21: Zalando generates >€10B in GMV across European online fashion, but operates with razor-thin operating margins (2-4%) and sub-hurdle multi-year ROIC (<8%). Apparel e-commerce is highly discretionary and sensitive to consumer sentiment. In addition, structural platform economics are impaired by high logistics/return costs and intense competition from low-cost Chinese platforms (Shein, Temu) and direct-to-consumer brand distribution.

column11: Societal and legislative acceptance risk; addictive gambling and sports betting business model facing recurring regulatory tightening, taxation increases, and severe compliance penalties.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). Addictive commercial gambling and sports betting model faces existential societal, legislative, and taxation risks. Ongoing regulatory tightening in the UK and Europe, compounded by past compliance scandals and massive penalty settlements.
column21: Entain operates global B2C sportsbooks and casinos (Ladbrokes, Coral, bwin, 50% BetMGM). Commercial gambling is inherently predatory and addictive, subjecting the company to severe regulatory crackdowns (UK stake caps, affordability checks, advertising restrictions) and taxation hikes. Historically, Entain has engaged in aggressive debt-funded M&A, suffered a massive £585M HMRC settlement in 2023 over historical Turkish operations, and faced substantial goodwill impairments.

column11: Societal and legislative acceptance risk; addictive online casino gambling infrastructure with ~60% of revenues derived from unregulated/gray jurisdictions (predominantly Asia) subject to sudden regulatory crackdowns and enforcement actions.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). B2B live online casino software and studio provider is exposed to severe societal and regulatory acceptance risks. Approximately 60% of revenues are derived from unregulated/gray markets (led by Asia at ~39%), creating extreme vulnerability to regulatory bans, payment blocking, and enforcement crackdowns.
column21: Evolution AB is the global market leader in B2B live dealer casino streaming with industry-leading EBITDA margins (>60%) and high ROIC. However, casino gambling is inherently addictive, and Evolution derives roughly 60% of total revenue from unregulated markets (predominantly Asia at ~€800M+). This exposes the company to existential regulatory and jurisdictional risks, including payment gateway restrictions, cyber-attacks, and sudden governmental prohibitions on online gambling.

column11: Societal and legislative acceptance risk; gambling, lottery, and sports-betting operations facing recurring state sin taxes, regulatory interventions, and public health scrutiny.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). Commercial gambling and lottery operations face chronic societal and legislative acceptance risk, including recurring tax increases ('sin taxes') and stringent regulatory restrictions. The €2.45B Kindred acquisition expands exposure to competitive and heavily regulated European online gaming.
column21: FDJ holds an exclusive 25-year French monopoly on retail lotteries and sports betting (until 2044), which is highly cash-generative. However, gambling is an addictive, socially sensitive activity subject to heavy state taxation (over 50% of gross gaming revenue collected by the French government in levies) and strict player-protection limits. Furthermore, the acquisition of Kindred Group (Unibet) significantly increases group exposure to competitive, highly regulated online sports betting and casino markets across Europe.

column11: Societal / legislative acceptance risk (addictive or predatory model).
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Lottomatica operates Italian online gaming, sports betting, and retail gaming machines (VLT/AWP). As an addictive and socially sensitive gambling business, it fails the Munger essential need standard and carries acute legislative, regulatory taxation, and concession renewal risks.
column21: Market leader in Italian online gaming (~31-32% share) and retail franchise networks under state concessions issued by the ADM. Generated >€2.25B in revenue with ~€2.1B net debt (~2.4x Net Debt/EBITDA). Operating under state licenses exposes the business to regulatory tax hikes, advertising bans, and tender renewal uncertainties, creating severe societal and legislative ruin risk.

column11: Non-essential / easily forgone product or service.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Logitech designs computer peripherals (mice, keyboards, webcams, gaming accessories). While high-quality and asset-light, PC peripherals represent deferrable, non-essential consumer hardware with multi-year replacement cycles, exhibiting severe post-pandemic cyclical contraction with zero deprivation pain.
column21: Global market leader in PC peripherals and gaming accessories with ~$4.3B in net sales in FY2024. Revenue surged during the 2020-2021 WFH boom before declining sharply by ~15-20% in FY2023 and an additional 5% in FY2024 as consumers and enterprise IT channels worked through inventory. Hardware upgrades are easily deferred for years, failing Munger's non-discretionary essential everyday habit standard.

column14: Local depot density and route logistics provide modest distribution scale, but post-tax GAAP ROIC is sub-hurdle at ~8-10% (well below the 12% Munger threshold) with razor-thin operating margins (~3-4%). As a bulk fuel/LPG distributor, pricing power is limited to a thin delivery markup over volatile commodity costs.
column20: Fails Gate 3 (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). While heating fuel and LPG delivery fulfill an essential physical need, DCC operates as a high-volume, low-margin distributor with thin ~3-4% operating margins and a multi-year post-tax ROIC below the 12% hurdle (~8-10%). It lacks independent pricing power against commodity swings and faces long-term structural volume headwinds from European building decarbonization and the energy transition.
column21: International energy distribution and services group with over £14B continuing revenue (transitioning to pure-play DCC Energy after divesting Healthcare and Technology). Historical ROCE/ROIC hovers around 8-11% post-tax. Although cash conversion is consistently high (>90-100%), the business is constrained by commodity price pass-through dynamics and thin ~3.5% adjusted operating margins.

column14: Regional distribution contracts and logistics density provide outsourced scale in small and emerging markets, but Inchcape possesses no structural pricing power against global OEMs (who dictate wholesale terms, hold contract cancellation rights, and can shift to direct-to-consumer/agency sales). Profitability remains vulnerable to OEM contract renegotiations and aggressive EV market discounting.
column20: Fails Gate 3 (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Inchcape provides outsourced vehicle distribution for global automotive OEMs (Toyota, BMW, Mercedes, BYD). However, OEMs hold the whip hand with unilateral contract renewal power, margin control, and the ability to disintermediate distributors via direct-to-consumer models, leaving Inchcape without an enduring pricing power moat.
column21: Pure-play global automotive distributor operating across 40+ markets following the Derco acquisition and divestment of UK retail. Operating margins sit at ~5.5-6.3%. While asset-light distribution yields high ROCE on a narrow capital base, Inchcape is structurally dependent on third-party OEM distribution agreements without proprietary toll booth protections or pricing power over vehicle MSRPs.

column14: Pearson VUE and UK qualification awarding bodies (Edexcel) operate as secure testing and certification toll booths, but 5-year median GAAP Return on Capital/ROIC is sub-hurdle at ~10.3% (7.9% in 2021 to 11.3% in 2025, failing the >=12% Munger threshold). Furthermore, higher education courseware and learning content face long-term pricing compression and generative AI disintermediation.
column20: Fails Gate 3 (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). While Pearson VUE computer-based testing and accredited examinations provide a strong testing toll booth, Pearson's 5-year median GAAP Return on Capital/ROIC is sub-hurdle at ~10.3% (consistently below 12% across 2021-2025), burdened by historical intangible asset acquisitions. Learning content also faces persistent pricing headwind from generative AI automation.
column21: Global learning and assessment provider generating ~£3.5-3.8B in revenue with adjusted operating margins improving from 11.2% in 2021 to ~17% in 2024-2025. Reported Return on Capital was 7.9% (2021), 8.7% (2022), 10.3% (2023), 10.5% (2024), and 11.3% (2025), failing the 12% multi-year hurdle required for empirical proof of moat under Gate 3b.

column14: Extensive store network (B&Q, Castorama, Screwfix) and own-brand sourcing provide retail purchasing scale, but 5-year median GAAP ROIC is deeply sub-hurdle at ~5-7% (far below the 12% threshold). Big-box DIY retail suffers from intense price competition, heavy lease liabilities, and lack of customer lock-in.
column20: Fails Gate 3 (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Kingfisher operates home improvement retail across the UK, France, and Poland, but generates structurally weak capital returns with multi-year ROIC hovering at only 5-7% and thin 3.5-6.5% operating margins. Highly exposed to cyclical housing turnover and consumer DIY pullbacks, it lacks genuine pricing power against discounters and online rivals.
column21: Multi-banner home improvement retailer with >2,000 stores across 8 European countries generating ~£13B in revenue. Group operating margins fluctuate between 3.5% and 6.5%. ROIC consistently prints in the 5-7% range, trailing its ~8% cost of capital. Substantial operating lease obligations and heavy store overhead prevent high-return capital compounding.

column11: Discretionary big-ticket purchase deferrable in recessions; cyclical residential homebuilder exposed to mortgage rates and housing cycle.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). Residential home purchases are discretionary, big-ticket, deferrable capital commitments that exhibit extreme cyclicality tied to mortgage borrowing costs, macro real estate cycles, and consumer confidence. Despite Berkeley's differentiated urban brownfield regeneration focus in London and the South East and disciplined long-term capital returns, cyclical homebuilders are explicitly excluded under Munger's non-deferrable everyday necessity standard.
column21: Berkeley Group operates primarily in London, Birmingham, and the South of England, specializing in complex, multi-year brownfield regeneration projects. While historically generating superior returns on capital relative to volume peers (ROCE historically 15-20% in cycle peaks), operating performance contracted sharply during the 2022-2024 mortgage rate spike, with reservation rates dropping over 30% and pre-tax profits declining from £604M in FY23 to £557M in FY24 and guided lower into FY25. The business faces structural planning constraints, multi-hundred-million-pound building safety / cladding remediation levies, and prolonged capital cycles where capital is tied up in multi-year landbanks. Under the Munger framework, private homebuilding represents a deferrable, highly cyclical big-ticket capital commitment rather than an entrenched daily habit or non-deferrable functional necessity.

column11: Discretionary big-ticket purchase deferrable in recessions; cyclical residential homebuilder exposed to mortgage rates and housing cycle.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). UK's largest volume housebuilder following the 2024 Barratt-Redrow merger. New home purchases are discretionary, big-ticket commitments that buyers defer during interest rate spikes and recessions. As a cyclical volume homebuilder exposed to UK mortgage rates, consumer affordability, and planning bottlenecks, it fails Munger's non-deferrable essential need standard.
column21: Barratt Redrow (formed via the £2.5B acquisition of Redrow by Barratt Developments in 2024) delivers ~14,000 homes annually across the UK. During the 2022-2024 rate shock, completions fell over 20% (Barratt standalone completions dropped from 17,206 in FY23 to 14,004 in FY24), operating margins collapsed from ~16-18% peak down to ~7-9%, and ROCE plummeted from ~25-30% in peak Help-to-Buy years to single digits (<8% in FY24). In addition, building safety and cladding remediation provisions exceed £600M cumulative. The merger adds integration execution risk and overheads to an already capital-intensive, cyclical volume builder model with no pricing power over mortgage rate swings.

column11: Discretionary big-ticket purchase deferrable in recessions; cyclical residential homebuilder exposed to mortgage rates and housing cycle.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). National UK volume housebuilder. Residential home purchases are discretionary, deferrable big-ticket capital commitments highly sensitive to mortgage rates and general economic confidence. Cyclical homebuilders are explicitly excluded under Munger's non-deferrable everyday necessity standard.
column21: Bellway p.l.c. is a major UK housebuilder operating across England, Scotland, and Wales. Completions plunged 30% from 10,945 in FY23 to 7,654 in FY24 following the UK mortgage rate surge. Operating margins shrank from 16.0% in FY23 to ~10.0% in FY24, and pre-tax profit fell over 50% to £226M. While Bellway maintains a relatively conservative balance sheet with net cash (£10M-£50M) and disciplined land buying, its financial returns fluctuate wildly across the economic cycle (ROCE falling from >20% in 2021-2022 to <8% in 2024). It possesses no pricing power to counteract build-cost inflation or mortgage-driven buyer deferrals.

column11: Discretionary big-ticket purchase deferrable in recessions; cyclical residential homebuilder exposed to mortgage rates and housing cycle.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). UK volume housebuilder focused on entry-level and first-time buyer housing. Home purchases are discretionary, highly deferrable big-ticket commitments that dried up following the withdrawal of Help-to-Buy and mortgage rate surges. Fails Munger's non-deferrable essential need standard.
column21: Persimmon plc is one of the largest UK volume housebuilders, operating through Persimmon Homes, Charles Church, and Westbury Partnerships. Operating profits collapsed by ~65% from £1.01B in 2022 to £355M in 2023 and remained subdued in 2024 as new home completions plummeted from 14,868 to 9,922 following the expiration of government Help-to-Buy subsidies and rising mortgage rates. Underlying ROCE collapsed from peak levels above 30% down to ~8-10%. Persimmon has historically suffered from build-quality controversies and customer service scandals, alongside multi-hundred-million cladding remediation liabilities. It represents an archetypal interest-rate-sensitive cyclical homebuilder lacking an unassailable economic moat.

column11: Discretionary big-ticket purchase deferrable in recessions; cyclical residential homebuilder exposed to mortgage rates and housing cycle.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). Major UK volume residential developer with large land holdings. New home purchasing is a discretionary, deferrable big-ticket commitment subject to severe mortgage-rate sensitivity and housing cycle volatility. Cyclical homebuilders fail Munger's non-deferrable everyday necessity standard.
column21: Taylor Wimpey plc is a UK national housebuilder operating across England, Scotland, and Wales, with a small operation in Spain. Group completions dropped from 14,154 homes in 2022 to 10,848 in 2023 and ~10,400 in 2024 as mortgage borrowing costs surged. Operating profit dropped ~50% from £923M in 2022 to £470M in 2023, with operating margins falling from 20.9% to ~13.4% and ROCE retreating from 25.1% to ~11.8% (and further into single digits in 2024). The company holds a large strategic landbank (~80,000 plots) requiring substantial capital tied up through planning cycles, and faces hundreds of millions in building safety and cladding remediation obligations. It possesses no structural pricing power over mortgage rate swings or planning system delays.

column11: Discretionary and deferrable travel/hospitality service; highly cyclical lodging spend easily forgone or traded down in economic downturns.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (REJECT). Hotel lodging and hospitality represent discretionary, deferrable travel expenditures highly sensitive to global economic cycles, corporate travel budgets, and consumer leisure spending. Despite shifting to an asset-light management and franchise model across ~5,600 hotels, hotel room nights are easily forgone or traded down during downturns, failing Munger's non-deferrable essential need standard.
column21: Accor SA is a French multinational hospitality franchisor and manager operating over 5,600 hotels across 110+ countries under 45+ brands (including Ibis, Novotel, Mercure, Sofitel, Pullman, and Fairmont). While its asset-light transition (divesting owned real estate via AccorInvest) has reduced maintenance capex intensity, group earnings and RevPAR remain deeply cyclical and tethered to discretionary travel demand. During the pandemic, group revenues dropped by over 50% and operating earnings swung to severe losses. Even post-recovery, historical ROIC has hovered between 5% and 8%, failing to reliably clear the 12% capital efficiency hurdle. Furthermore, Accor faces severe distribution pressure from online travel agency gatekeepers (Booking Holdings, Expedia) and alternative accommodation platforms (Airbnb), diluting brand pricing power.

column11: Discretionary leisure and corporate travel is non-essential and deferrable in economic downturns; hotel lodging does not meet the essential Western need or high-frequency everyday habit standard.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). While IHG operates an asset-light franchise fee model, hotel lodging is fundamentally discretionary leisure and corporate travel that is deferrable during economic recessions, failing the essential Western need standard.
column21: IHG operates ~920k rooms across 19 brands with >70% of operating profit from franchise royalties. However, end-market demand is driven by cyclical travel, resulting in severe RevPAR collapses during downturns (-52% in 2020). Historical debt-funded share repurchases also led to negative book equity and elevated leverage (~5.5x Net Debt/NI).

column11: Package holiday tours, leisure airlines, and cruise ship operations are pure discretionary big-ticket travel, explicitly disqualifying under Gate 2.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). TUI operates leisure airlines, cruise lines, and package tour operations, representing big-ticket discretionary holiday spending that is completely deferrable during economic stress and explicitly disqualified under Gate 2.
column21: TUI's business spans airlines, cruise lines (TUI Cruises, Marella), and package tour operators. Demand is intensely cyclical and consumer-discretionary. Operating margins are historically razor-thin (2-4%), and the company required billions in German state bailouts (WSF) and catastrophic equity dilution to survive the 2020 pandemic downturn.

column11: Budget hotel accommodation is non-essential and subject to discretionary travel cycles that are easily forgone during economic downturns.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Whitbread operates the Premier Inn budget hotel chain; budget lodging is non-essential and subject to discretionary leisure and business travel cycles that are cut during economic recessions.
column21: Whitbread operates >85k rooms under Premier Inn, largely through a capital-intensive freehold/leasehold owner-operator model. Its ROCE/ROIC hovers around 8-11%, depressed by heavy real estate assets and German expansion capex. End-market lodging demand is cyclical and discretionary, failing Gate 2 essential need requirements.

column11: Premium espresso machines and small domestic appliances are discretionary consumer durables with multi-year replacement cycles, easily deferred during economic downturns.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). De'Longhi designs and manufactures premium espresso machines and small domestic kitchen appliances; these are discretionary consumer durables with multi-year replacement cycles that are easily deferred in economic downturns, failing the essential Western need standard.
column21: While De'Longhi has built a strong brand presence in bean-to-cup coffee makers and commercial espresso (La Marzocco, Eversys) generating ~12% operating margins and a net cash balance sheet, >65% of revenue comes from consumer household appliances. These represent discretionary durable goods subject to replacement cycles and retail channel bargaining power (MediaMarkt, Amazon), rather than essential high-frequency consumable purchases.

column11: Tabletop fantasy miniatures and wargaming are pure discretionary hobby/entertainment products that are completely deferrable in downturns, failing the essential Western need standard.
