column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Despite world-class capital efficiency (>100% ROIC, zero debt, >40% operating margins), Games Workshop's Warhammer tabletop wargaming miniatures are pure discretionary hobby products that are completely deferrable and non-essential.
column21: Games Workshop generates extraordinary financial returns (>100% GAAP ROIC, zero long-term debt, >100% FCF conversion) via vertically integrated miniature manufacturing, retail stores, and Warhammer IP licensing. However, end demand is centered entirely on a discretionary tabletop hobby, failing Gate 2's essential Western need or broad entrenched everyday habit criteria.

column11: Listing country Greece is pre-screened as in_market == 'N'; furthermore, discount seasonal toys and home goods are non-essential discretionary retail products.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Listing country Greece is classified outside core Western developed markets (in_market == 'N'); additionally, Jumbo's discount toys, seasonal items, and home knick-knacks represent non-essential discretionary retail.
column21: Jumbo operates ~85 discount hyperstores across Greece, Romania, Bulgaria, and Cyprus selling toys, seasonal merchandise, and home decor. While generating robust gross margins (~53%) and maintaining a net cash balance sheet, Greece carries in_market == 'N' pre-screen status, and merchandise demand is exposed to discretionary consumer spending cycles in Southeastern Europe.

column14: Foodbuy procurement scale delivers food and supplies at costs unobtainable by regional competitors, passing savings to clients while contract escalators protected margins during 2022-2024 inflation with >96% retention.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global market leader in contract foodservice leveraging Foodbuy procurement scale to drive first-time outsourcing wins across healthcare, education, and corporate dining. Contractual escalators passed through high inflation with >96% retention. Sound balance sheet with net debt ~2.0x NI and >7.8x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: net new outsourcing wins 3.5% + like-for-like volume/price 3.0% + margin expansion 0.5% + net share buybacks 1.0%]
column21: Consistently achieves 18-22% GAAP ROIC over multi-year cycles (median 19.1%). Owner FCF conversion exceeds 120% of net income ($2.43B FCF vs $1.87B NI in FY25). Foodbuy purchasing power aggregates massive volume, establishing an insurmountable cost advantage over regional peers.

column14: While Sodexo possesses global catering scale, its multi-year GAAP ROIC (6-8%) and operating margins (3-5%) consistently fall far short of the 12% hurdle. Lacks the food procurement scale and execution efficiency of Compass Group, with returns diluted by facilities management.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Proof of Moat). Despite global contract catering presence, 5-year GAAP ROIC sits at ~6-8% and operating margins at 3.3-4.7%, well below the 12% hurdle. Lags peer Compass Group substantially in North American procurement scale, operating efficiency, and contractual pricing leverage.
column21: Reported GAAP ROIC was 6.1% in FY23 and 7.7% in FY24, with operating profit margins hovering between 3.3% and 4.7%. Even after spinning off high-margin voucher business Pluxee in early 2024, core on-site catering and facilities management fail to demonstrate economic moat returns.

column11: Primary listing and operations in Poland/CEE outside approved Western developed market universe (in_market=N), alongside discretionary non-essential nature of corporate gym benefit cards.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Essential Need & Market Mandate). Disqualified by pre-screen geographic condition as Poland is outside the approved rule-of-law Western developed market universe (in_market=N). Furthermore, employer-subsidized sports cards are non-essential discretionary corporate perks subject to corporate belt-tightening.
column21: Listed on the Warsaw Stock Exchange with the bulk of revenue and fitness card memberships generated across Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, and Bulgaria (in_market=N). Although it possesses strong regional network effects with the MultiSport card, it fails the Western developed market mandate.

column14: Local food delivery marketplace density does not generate durable pricing power or switching barriers; consumer and merchant multi-homing is rampant, and 5-year median GAAP ROIC is deeply negative amidst heavy promotional subsidies.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Proof of Moat). Long history of GAAP operating losses and deeply negative 5-year median ROIC. Lacks structural pricing power due to low customer loyalty, merchant multi-homing, high marketing subsidies, and escalating regulatory pressure on gig-economy courier models.
column21: Multi-year GAAP net income has been consistently negative with cumulative net losses exceeding several billion euros over the last 5 years. Only achieved positive group FCF (~€100M) in FY24 after aggressive cost cuts and capital restructuring. Relies on subsidiary divestments and listings (e.g. Talabat in UAE) rather than organic self-funding economic moats.

column14: Premium tire brand equity and specialized engineering know-how, but commodity passenger and commercial replacement tires face fierce price competition from low-cost Asian imports while auto OEMs squeeze margins, capping 5-year median GAAP ROIC at 11.1% (below the 12% hurdle).
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Proof of Moat). Despite premium brand equity and specialty tire R&D, 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 11.1% fails the 12% hurdle (deteriorating to 9.8% in FY25). Structural price competition from low-cost Asian manufacturers in the replacement market and automotive OEM bargaining power prevent sustained pricing power.
column21: GAAP ROIC has steadily faded from 11.8% in 2022 to 11.6% in 2023, 10.6% in 2024, and 9.8% in 2025 (median 11.1%). Tangible ROIC slipped to 13.0% in FY25. Revenues contracted from €28.6B in FY22 to €26.0B in FY25, and Owner EPS fell from €2.79 to €2.34, failing peak-to-peak compounding.

column14: High-value prestige tire positioning and Formula 1 sponsorship create brand recognition, but GAAP ROIC of ~6-7% (obscured by non-GAAP adjustments excluding €4.5B+ buyout intangibles) fails the 12% hurdle; vulnerable to automotive OEM price pressure and raw material inflation cycles.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Proof of Moat). Premium and prestige tire focus fails to deliver the required 12% GAAP ROIC. While Pirelli reports adjusted non-GAAP 'ROIC' of >20%, this excludes over €4.5B in acquisition intangibles and goodwill; true GAAP ROIC is ~6-7%. Lacks durable pricing power above raw material inflation cycles.
column21: Reported GAAP net income of ~€470-500M on total invested capital of ~€7.7B (equity €5.76B + net financial debt €1.93B) results in GAAP ROIC of ~6.1-6.5% and ROE of ~8.1%, far below the 12% threshold. In addition, corporate governance is complicated by Sinochem's 37% stake and Italian government Golden Power restrictions.

column14: Unrivaled global brewing scale and dominant #1 volume share in key profit pools (Latin America, US, Africa). Pricing power demonstrated through consistent positive price/mix, though challenged by brand erosion in US Bud Light.
column20: Fails Gate 5 (Management Score = 0, REJECT). Disastrous capital allocation legacy from the $103B debt-fueled SABMiller acquisition in 2016 which impaired shareholder returns for a decade, forced multiple dividend cuts, and left an unwieldy debt burden ($67B+ net debt). Further exacerbated by the 2023 Bud Light marketing misstep that permanently forfeited #1 US market share.
column21: Net debt of $67.6B (~2.9x EBITDA, >12x net income) remains elevated 8+ years post-SABMiller. 5-year GAAP ROIC depressed at 7-9%. In 2023, Bud Light lost over 25% of its sales volume in the US following marketing backlash, ceding the #1 US beer title to Constellation's Modelo Especial. Non-GAAP normalized adjustments routinely mask underlying equity stagnation.

column14: Dense regional brewery footprint and dominant route-to-market distribution in the Nordics, Western Europe, and high-growth Asian markets (China #1 in Western provinces, Vietnam, India). Demonstrated pricing power via premiumization and non-alcoholic portfolio.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Leading international brewer with dominant Nordic and Western European route-to-market scale and rapid Asian expansion (China, Vietnam, India). Strong pricing power with ROIC of 14.5% (37.6% tangible). Britvic acquisition expands non-alcoholic platform. Balance sheet leverage manageable with swift deleveraging track record. [5-10Y g: volume 1.0% + price/mix 2.5% + Asia/Britvic expansion 1.5% - margin drag 0.5% + buybacks 1.0%]
column21: 2024 ROIC reported at 14.5% (ex-goodwill 37.6%). NIBD/EBITDA stood at 1.65x in 2024 before the £3.3B Britvic transaction, with management targeting <2.5x leverage post-close. FCF conversion routinely exceeds 85%. Carlsberg Foundation ownership ensures long-term stewardship and prevents value-destroying mega-M&A.

column14: Global brand leadership anchored by the flagship Heineken brand (#1 international premium beer) and entrenched local distribution infrastructure across 190+ markets. Demonstrated pricing power through premiumization, price/mix pass-through, and pioneering zero-alcohol (Heineken 0.0).
column20: Passes all 6 gates. World's #2 brewer with the most international premium brand portfolio. Proven pricing power with positive price/mix offsetting inflationary pressures. Robust cash generation with >€3B free operating cash flow and net debt/EBITDA of 2.2x under prudent family control. [5-10Y g: volume 1.5% + price/mix 2.5% + premium/0.0% mix 1.0% - input margin drag 0.5% + buybacks/dividends 0.5%]
column21: Organic operating profit grew 8.3% in 2024 with organic net revenue up 5%. Free operating cash flow reached €3.0B+, driving net debt to EBITDA down to 2.2x. Operating tangible ROIC exceeds 15%. Heineken 0.0 commands leadership in non-alcoholic beer globally, insulating against volume moderation trends.

column14: Look-through ownership of Heineken N.V. (50.005% controlling interest): world's #1 international premium beer brand, dense multi-continent distribution, and proven pricing power through cycle.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Pure holding company holding a 50.005% controlling interest in Heineken N.V., providing identical look-through brewing economics at an attractive holding company discount. Family governance ensures generational alignment and balance sheet prudence. [5-10Y g: look-through volume 1.5% + price/mix 2.5% + premium/0.0% mix 1.0% - input margin drag 0.5% + holding yield 0.5%]
column21: Heineken Holding holds 50.005% of Heineken N.V. with negligible standalone debt or corporate overhead. Look-through operating performance reflects Heineken N.V.'s 8.3% organic profit growth, €3.0B+ FCF, and 2.2x net debt/EBITDA. Dividends received from Heineken N.V. are mirrored directly to holding shareholders.

column14: Strong regional market share and local route-to-market distribution in the Nordics, Baltics, and Italy across beer, malt beverages, and soft drinks. Moderate pricing power in home territories.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). Regional multi-niche beverage model lacks global brand scale and faces saturated, zero-growth domestic markets in the Nordics and Baltics. Organic runway is structurally constrained, forcing reliance on debt-funded cross-border bolt-on acquisitions in mature markets to sustain growth.
column21: Royal Unibrew holds solid regional positions in Denmark, Finland, and the Baltics, but organic volume growth is near zero due to demographic maturity. Growth has been heavily reliant on acquisitions (e.g., Vrumona in the Netherlands, Norkhald, San Giorgio), increasing leverage and execution risk without establishing durable global moat barriers.

column11: General merchandise discount variety retailer with substantial discretionary, seasonal, and easily deferrable product assortment.
column20: Fails Gate 2 (Rejected – G2 Essential Need). Operates a discount variety retail chain heavily exposed to discretionary general merchandise, seasonal goods, and impulse purchases that are easily forgone during economic downturns. Lacks essential staple demand or entrenched everyday habit lock-in.
column21: Discretionary non-grocery categories (homeware, seasonal, toys, DIY) represent a large portion of B&M's sales and the vast majority of its gross profit. Like-for-like sales volatility and customer spending pullbacks during inflationary periods demonstrate that the assortment is deferrable rather than an essential everyday necessity.

column14: High street retail price-taker in a hyper-competitive UK grocery and apparel market. Lacks defensible switching costs or scale economies shared against discounters (Aldi, Lidl) and dominant supermarket chains (Tesco, Sainsbury's). 5-year median GAAP ROIC (~7-8%) sits far below the 12% hurdle, with Food operating margins constrained to ~4-5% and exposed to UK national living wage increases and business rates.
column20: Fails Gate 3 (Moat Archetype = None, 3b = N, REJECT). UK department and grocery retailer lacks pricing power and defensible structural barriers against discounters (Aldi/Lidl) and online apparel competitors. 5-year median GAAP ROIC (~7-8%) sits well below the 12% hurdle despite recent turnaround progress.
column21: Operating margins in Food hover at ~4.7-5.4% while Fashion/Home reaches ~10-11%, but multi-year GAAP ROIC has averaged ~7-8% over the full 2020-2024 cycle due to lease liabilities, Ocado Retail JV write-downs, and structural UK living wage pressures. Retail price-taker lacking durable pricing power above inflation.

column14: Owns iconic Italian aperitif brands (Aperol, Campari) with proprietary recipes and cultural Lindy cachet. However, fails Gate 3b proof of moat: 5-year and 10-year median GAAP ROIC has structurally hovered at 7-8%, well below the 12% hurdle, diluted by goodwill-heavy acquisitions (Grand Marnier, €1.2B Courvoisier buyout) and high A&P spend required to maintain Aperol spritz momentum against cocktail fashion shifts.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Proof of Moat & Pricing, REJECT). While Aperol and Campari possess strong cultural brand cachet, Campari fails Gate 3b with 5-year and 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 7-8%, failing the 12% hurdle. Returns diluted by expensive debt-funded M&A (Courvoisier) and high marketing reinvestment. Does not qualify for Calamity Tier as sub-12% ROIC is structural across the multi-year cycle.
column21: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~7.8%, with recent ROIC compressing toward ~5.4-6.1%. Net debt rose to €2.28B post the €1.2B Courvoisier acquisition, pushing net leverage to ~3.5x-3.9x EBITDA. Consecutive CEO transitions in 2024 (Bob Kunze-Concewitz stepping down, followed by Matteo Fantacchiotti abruptly exiting after 5 months) further eroded capital allocation consistency.

column14: Dominant global spirits leader owning irreplaceable aged Scotch maturation inventory and distilleries across Scotland protected by statutory geographical indication, alongside iconic Lindy mega-brands (Johnnie Walker, Guinness, Don Julio). Proof of moat demonstrated by 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 14-16% and operating margins of 28-30%.
column19: Broken metric: Gate 5 score of 0 due to pro-cyclical share repurchases executed at peak valuations (£38-£40), major distributor overstocking in Latin America & Caribbean, and leadership instability culminating in CEO Debra Crew's July 2025 exit. Moat proof: World #1 spirits franchise (#1 Scotch Johnnie Walker, Guinness booming globally) with unreplicable aged inventory; 5-year median GAAP ROIC remains 14-16% through the downturn. Fix catalyst & kill-switch: 2025 leadership reset enforcing real-time POS sell-out tracking, cost productivity targets, and halting buybacks to prioritize debt reduction to <2.5x net debt/EBITDA; kill switch if ROIC falls below 12% or net leverage exceeds 3.5x for more than two consecutive reporting cycles.
column20: Qualifies for Calamity Tier (Gate 5 management failure waived as temporary fixable calamity; Anchor Gates 1, 2, 3a, 4 and Gate 6 pass). World #1 spirits leader anchored by irreplaceable aged Scotch stocks and Guinness stout. Multi-cycle ROIC remains resilient at 14-16% despite Latin America destocking shock. Strong balance sheet with interest coverage >6.5x. [5-10Y g: spirits volume 1.5% + premiumisation price 2.0% + Guinness expansion 1.0% - promotional margin drag 0.5% + net debt repayment 1.0%]
column21: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~15.8% (FY20: 16.1%, FY22: 18.4%, FY23: 19.8%, FY24: 15.8%, FY25: 13.7%). Operating margins steady at 28-30%. FCF conversion >85% of net income. Net debt/EBITDA ~2.8x with interest coverage of ~6.8x. Channel inventory in Latin America normalized by late FY25.

column14: Unreplicable aged cognac (Martell), Scotch whisky (Chivas Regal, The Glenlivet), and Irish whiskey (Jameson) maturation inventories tied to statutory protected regions and centuries-old distillation terroir. Tangible operating ROIC exceeds 20% on physical operating capital, with demonstrated pricing power through positive price/mix realization across the business cycle.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. World #2 premium spirits group anchored by protected-origin aged cognac, Scotch, and Irish whiskey inventories. Tangible operating ROIC >20% on physical capital with multi-cycle pricing power. Net debt/EBITDA ~3.1x and interest coverage >6.5x provide peace-of-mind solvency through industry downturns. [5-10Y g: global volume 1.0% + premium price 2.0% + aged mix 1.5% - China tariff drag 0.5% + net buyback/deleveraging 1.0%]
column21: Tangible ROIC >20% (Recurring operating profit ~€3.3B on ~€13B PPE and operating working capital, though GAAP ROIC is 6-8% due to €18B accounting goodwill from Allied Domecq/Absolut). Multi-year FCF conversion ~80%. Net debt of €6.34B represents ~3.1x EBITDA with EBIT/interest coverage of 6.7x. Divestment of lower-margin wine brands refocuses capital on high-margin spirits.

column14: Operates dense regional grocery store networks across the US East Coast (Food Lion, Stop & Shop, Giant) and Benelux (Albert Heijn). It has no ability to protect margins in a depressed commodity tape.

column20: Fails Gate 3b (Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT). Regional Iberian integrated energy operator and non-operated upstream participant (Brazil pre-salt, Namibia Mopane discovery). Operating cash flows and returns on capital are dictated by Brent crude prices, natural gas benchmarks, and volatile European refining crack spreads.
column21: Galp operates three core divisions: Upstream (offshore production in Brazil pre-salt Santos Basin and exploration in Namibia's Orange Basin), Industrial & Midstream (Sines refinery with 220 kbpd capacity and natural gas supply), and Commercial (1,200+ service stations and power/gas retail across Iberia). While recent upstream cash flows have been strong due to favorable oil pricing and low extraction costs in Brazil (<$5/boe operating cost), historical ROIC displays severe cyclicality: normalized 10-year ROIC averages ~8-10%, with sharp compressions during oil downturns (e.g. 2020 net loss of -€42M and ROIC <4%). Downstream refining margins fluctuate uncontrollably based on regional supply-demand imbalances, and retail fuel distribution operates in a competitive, price-sensitive environment. Galp has zero ability to raise prices independently of global commodity benchmarks without forfeiting market share.

column14: Commodity price-taker across upstream oil and gas, basic petrochemicals, and polyolefins. Lacks pricing power to independently raise prices above inflation; earnings are held hostage to Brent crude, European TTF natural gas prices, and cyclical polyolefin chemical spreads.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT). Integrated Central European energy and chemicals producer. While OMV's inland refineries (Schwechat, Burghausen) enjoy logistical insulation and its Borealis chemical arm provides downstream integration, it remains an unhedged commodity price-taker across crude, natural gas, and cyclical polyolefins. Multi-cycle returns on capital fall well short of the 12% Munger hurdle during down-cycles, exacerbated by past geopolitical missteps and Russian gas supply disruption.
column21: OMV operates across three segments: Energy (upstream exploration & production in Norway, Romania, and the Middle East), Fuels & Feedstock (refineries in Austria, Germany, and Romania with ~17.8 mtpa refining capacity), and Chemicals & Materials (Borealis polyolefins and specialty polymers, plus Borouge JV). While the 2022-2023 energy spike produced windfall profits, OMV's multi-decade capital efficiency is deeply cyclical: 10-year median ROIC sits around 7-9%. In 2020, ROIC crashed below 4% and net income plunged to €1.48B (with heavy impairments), while 2022 was hit by a €2.5B write-down on Russian assets (Nord Stream 2 financing and Yuzhno-Russkoye upstream field). In chemicals, Borealis faces intense margin pressure from low-cost Middle Eastern and US ethane-based competitors. OMV has zero pricing power to pass through cost inflation in commodity polymers or retail fuels.

column20: Fails Gate 2 (Essential Western Need / Rule of Law & Governance, REJECT). Headquartered and listed in Poland (in_market == 'N'). While Orlen operates a domestic monopoly across refining, natural gas distribution (via PGNiG), and fuel retail, it is ~49.9% owned by the Polish State Treasury and historically functions as an arm of state industrial and social policy rather than a shareholder compounder. Subject to state-directed mergers, political board turnover, pre-election artificial fuel price freezes (autumn 2023), and heavy regulatory extraction.
column21: Orlen dominates Polish refining (Płock refinery), fuel retailing (3,100+ stations across Poland, Germany, Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary, and Lithuania), natural gas transmission/sales (PGNiG acquisition), and petrochemicals (Olefins III expansion). However, the Polish State Treasury holds a controlling ~49.9% equity stake, which has repeatedly overridden minority shareholder interests. Examples include: (1) political fuel discounting ahead of the October 2023 Polish parliamentary elections, causing nationwide fuel shortages and margin compression; (2) politically directed, dilutive state-sponsored mega-mergers with Grupa Lotos and PGNiG; (3) massive multi-billion-zloty cost overruns and subsequent write-downs on the Olefins III petrochemical complex; and (4) regulatory windfall levies and gas price compensation mechanisms controlled by the Polish government. Capital allocation is subordinated to national geopolitical and electoral objectives.

column14: Pure commodity price-taker. Upstream hydrocarbon production is sold at prevailing international market prices, while downstream refining profits are dictated by European crack spreads. Multi-cycle ROIC fails the 12% threshold due to severe cyclicality and non-recoverable impairment cycles.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT). Spanish integrated energy company with leading Iberian refining and retail distribution. Despite high-complexity refining assets and growing low-carbon power investments, Repsol is a structural commodity price-taker lacking pricing power above inflation. Financial performance is tethered to cyclical global crude benchmarks, Henry Hub gas prices, and volatile refining margins, compounded by Spanish government windfall energy taxes.
column21: Repsol operates across Upstream (crude and gas extraction in North America, Latin America, and North Africa), Industrial (5 refineries in Spain with ~1.0 mbpd capacity, large petrochemical complexes, and trading), and Commercial/Customer (retail marketing, mobility, and low-carbon electricity/gas generation). Multi-cycle ROIC is deeply cyclical and fails the 12% Munger bar across a full 10-year cycle: 10-year average ROIC is ~6-7%, characterized by massive write-downs during cyclical downturns (e.g., €3.8B impairment in 2019 anticipating decarbonization, and deep losses in 2020 with negative net income of -€3.29B). In 2022-2023, while refining margins surged temporarily, profits were heavily dampened by Spain's 1.2% windfall tax on energy revenue. Repsol possesses zero ability to raise fuel or chemical prices independently of spot market dynamics.

column14: Unmatched global LNG portfolio and trading scale, but fundamentally a commodity price-taker across crude oil, natural gas, refining crack spreads, and commodity chemicals. Lacks pricing power to independently raise prices above inflation; 10-year average ROIC of ~5.7% fails the 12% Munger hurdle.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT). Global integrated energy giant with market-leading positions in LNG liquefaction and global energy trading. Despite improved capital discipline under CEO Wael Sawan (focusing on high-margin upstream, divesting sub-hurdle European/Asian refining and retail assets), Shell is a structural commodity price-taker. Long-term returns on capital fall drastically short of the Munger standard, with a 10-year average ROIC of ~5.7% and a 5-year median of ~9.0% (<12% hurdle), governed by uncontrollable macro commodity price cycles.
column21: Shell operates across Integrated Gas (LNG, gas-to-liquids, and global trading), Upstream (deepwater and conventional oil/gas extraction), Marketing (mobility, lubricants, commercial fuels), and Chemicals & Products (refining and petrochemicals). Over a full 10-to-20-year economic cycle, Shell's capital efficiency fails the Munger hurdle: 10-year average ROIC is ~5.68%, 15-year average is ~5.65%, and 20-year average is ~6.61%. While ROIC spiked to ~16.9% in 2022 on the back of historic European gas and crude price spikes following the Ukraine invasion, it rapidly normalized to ~9.0% in 2023-2024 and ~8.3% in 2025. In down-cycles (such as 2015-2016 and 2020), returns collapsed toward zero (2020 GAAP net loss of -$21.7B due to $22B+ in post-tax impairments and dividend cut of 66%). Upstream oil, gas, and chemicals products have zero customer lock-in or pricing power above spot clearing rates.

column14: Lowest-cost upstream portfolio among Western supermajors and tier-1 global LNG trading scale, but fundamentally a commodity price-taker. Returns on capital fluctuate with Brent crude, natural gas, and refining margins; lacks independent pricing power to raise prices above inflation during industry downcycles.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT). Recognized as the most disciplined and lowest-cost operator among the European energy supermajors (upstream production costs <$5/boe, industry-leading peer ROACE of ~12.6% in 2025). However, TotalEnergies remains an unhedged commodity price-taker across crude oil, natural gas, and refining crack spreads. Long-term returns are dictated by global commodity swings, falling to low single digits during energy slumps (2020 ROIC <3%), with zero ability to raise prices independently of world benchmark prices.
column21: TotalEnergies operates across Exploration & Production (advantaged low-cost assets in the Middle East, West Africa, and Americas), Integrated LNG (world #3 LNG portfolio with major projects in Qatar, US, and Mozambique), Integrated Power (expanding solar, wind, and flexible gas generation), and Refining & Chemicals. Under CEO Patrick Pouyanné, capital allocation has been superior to peers, maintaining a low cash breakeven (<$25/boe). However, its economic returns remain tied to volatile commodity markets: 10-year average ROIC/ROACE hovers around 11-12%, experiencing severe cyclical valleys (2016 ROIC ~5-7%, 2020 GAAP net loss of -$7.2B with ROIC collapsing to ~2.5%) counterbalanced by 2022 windfall spikes (~19-24% ROIC). TotalEnergies sells standardized commodity units into open global auctions and cannot raise prices above inflation when market balances shift into oversupply.

column14: Dominates global LNG carrier membrane containment with 90-100% market share. Royalty toll of ~3-4% of vessel capex ($250M+) is low relative to catastrophic cryogenic failure risk (-163°C), creating insurmountable customer switching costs. Empirically proven by >50-70% ROIC and ~65% operating margin. Primary erosion threat is yard-backed proprietary designs (e.g. South Korea's KC-1/KC-2) which have repeatedly failed in commercial operation.
column20: Exceptional asset-light engineering monopoly on LNG carrier membrane containment (>90% market share). column20: Fails Gate 3b (Reject). column20: Fails Gate 6 (Peace-of-Mind Balance Sheet, REJECT). Under Munger's strict solvency standard, multi-line life liabilities fail the peace-of-mind test in a severe systemic crisis.
column21: FY2025 EBIT of €16.2B, GAAP ROIC of 18.9% (5Y median 17.2%), and Solvency II ratio of 218%. Common equity remains vulnerable to systemic credit freezes, violating the peace-of-mind balance sheet standard.

Multi-cycle economic ROIC fails the 12% hurdle.

Multi-cycle GAAP ROIC fails the 12% hurdle, and claims inflation volatility impairs underwriting returns.

[5-10Y g: Nordic premium volume 2.0% + tariff indexation 2.5% + combined ratio optimization 0.5% + capital return 1.5%]
column21: Over 200-year operating history in Norway with expanding positions in Denmark and Sweden. GAAP ROIC has steadily climbed from 14.8% (2022) to 23.6% (2025), with tangible ROIC exceeding 30%. Pre-tax profit plunged during the Covid-19 business interruption disputes where Hiscox faced major UK FCA court action. Return on equity in 2021 (8.1%) and 2022 (10.1%) failed the 12% cost-of-capital hurdle before rebounding during the 2023-2025 hard reinsurance market. Furthermore, net interest margins face terminal margin pressure from digital banking alternatives and Swiss National Bank rate cycle compression, limiting competitive advantage longevity below the required 15-year hurdle.
column21: Multi-cycle ROE has averaged 11.0-12.5% (12.5% in 2023, 11.5% in 2024, 11.0% in 2025) with a steady cost-to-income ratio of 53-56%. While BCVN possesses strong local solvency (CET1 >18%) and low historical credit loss provisions, its statutory public mandate binds operations to Canton de Vaud, eliminating external reinvestment runways. Fractional-reserve asset base (>CHF 55B on ~CHF 4B equity) exposes earnings power to central bank rate regimes and commoditized mortgage competition.

column14: Second/third-largest commercial bank and mortgage lender in Denmark with entrenched retail/commercial customer relationships, sticky operational deposits, and scale in covered bond mortgage origination (Jyske Realkredit). Demonstrated double-digit ROE (11.4-14.4% in 2023-2024) and cost-to-income ratio of 42-47% across normalized rate regimes.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). Danish universal commercial bank operating in a mature, highly concentrated oligopoly dominated by Danske Bank, Nordea, and Nykredit. Commercial banking is structurally anchored in Mauboussin Tier 4 (baseline CAP 5-10 years) due to rapid competitive return fade. Mortgage administration margins (bidragssatser) are subject to intense consumer and political scrutiny, while core net interest income faces cyclical headwinds as Danmarks Nationalbank cuts rates, truncating predictable moat runway below 15 years.
column21: FY2023 ROE reached 14.4% (ROTE 15.7%) before normalizing to 11.4% in FY2024 and ~10.5-11.5% in FY2025 as interest rate tailwinds subsided. Cost-to-income ratio rose from 42.5% in 2023 to ~48-50% in 2025. Danish mortgage system match-funding model reduces balance sheet duration risk but caps economic spreads on commoditized home loans. Geographic focus is strictly domestic Denmark with minimal secular growth avenues.

column14: Exceptional, decades-evolved lean credit culture and decentralized operational efficiency producing an elite cost-to-income ratio of ~25-26%, unmatched among European banks. Empirically proven by 5-year median ROIC of 18.6% and ROE >20% (21.0% in 2024, 22.4% in 2025), with virtually zero structural credit loss impairments across multi-decade business cycles.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). Ringkjøbing Landbobank is an extraordinarily well-managed niche bank, but under the Mauboussin outside-view persistence framework, commercial deposit banking possesses a structural baseline CAP of 5-10 years due to commoditized capital and credit cycle mean reversion. As a DKK 41B market cap Danish regional lender, its addressable runway is bounded by the Danish economy; expanding beyond its core regional footprint risks diluting its unique credit discipline and sub-26% cost culture. Capped at 10 years, failing the 15-year hurdle.
column21: Historical GAAP ROIC was 12.2% in 2022, 19.7% in 2023, 21.6% in 2024, and 17.5% in 2025 (5-year median 18.6%). Net income compounded from DKK 1,495M (2022) to DKK 2,313M (2025) with Owner EPS growing from 53.4 to 92.86 DKK (20.3% CAGR). Cost/income ratio remained world-class at 25.7% (2024) and 26.4% (2025). However, total loan assets are concentrated in Jutland/Copenhagen niche private banking and renewable energy/wind financing, leaving long-term reinvestment runway constrained by domestic Danish credit demand.

column14: Leading regional savings bank alliance in Southern and Western Norway following the merger of SpareBank 1 SR-Bank and SpareBank 1 Sørøst-Norge. Dominant retail deposit and SME lending market share combined with shared product development via SpareBank 1 Gruppen (insurance, asset management, payment solutions). Multi-year ROE sustained at 12.8-15.3% with an efficient cost-to-income ratio of ~37-38%.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). Commercial and regional savings banking sits in Mauboussin Tier 4 with high fade rates and baseline CAP of 5-10 years. SpareBank 1 Sør-Norge's earnings are heavily levered to the Norwegian regional economic cycle, commercial real estate, and energy/offshore industries. Net interest margins face structural headwinds as Norges Bank begins rate-cutting cycles, and post-merger integration risks constrain operating agility. Predictable moat runway cannot exceed 5 years.
column21: Reported consolidated ROE was 15.3% in 2023 (SR-Bank historical), 14.1% in 2024, and 12.8% in 2025 (~13.8% on tangible equity). Cost-to-income ratio remained well-controlled at 36.7% in 2024 and 38.0% in 2025. Total assets exceed NOK 400B funded predominantly by retail deposits and covered bonds (OMF). Reinvestment is bound to Norwegian domestic credit growth, with high cyclicality in offshore energy SME and commercial real estate lending portfolios.

column14: Created from the May 2025 merger of Sparebanken Vest and Sparebanken Sør to become Norway's largest independent savings bank. Entrenched deposit franchises across Western and Southern Norway with deep community roots, customer ownership certificate loyalty, and digital distribution via Bulder Bank. Normalized ROE / ROTE sustained between 12.7% and 16.0%.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). Commercial retail/SME banking exhibits high fade rates under the Mauboussin persistence framework (Tier 4, baseline CAP 5-10 years). While the merger of Sparebanken Vest and Sparebanken Sør creates significant regional scale in Western and Southern Norway, earnings remain cyclical, commoditized, and rate-sensitive. Integration of core banking systems, branch rationalization, and fierce competition from DNB and regional rivals limit competitive advantage longevity to 5 years.
column21: Reported headline ROE was 14.0% in Q2 2026 (16.0% adjusted for merger costs) and 12.7% in Q3 2026 (14.5% ROTE). Combined loan book spans retail residential mortgages (~75%) and regional SME/commercial lending (~25%). Digital challenger brand Bulder Bank drives retail customer acquisition but offers price-led commoditized mortgages with lower net interest margins. Geographic focus is confined to Norway with no international expansion potential.

column14: Fifth-largest bank in Spain with dominant branch and deposit density in Andalusia and Castile & León following the Liberbank integration. High switching costs in sticky rural and regional retail deposit accounts provide a low-cost funding base, supporting a rebound in ROTE to 10.4% in 2024 and adjusted ROTE of 12.1% in 2025.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). Regional retail banking in Spain is subject to intense commoditization, high regulatory/political intervention (such as the Spanish extraordinary bank tax), and cyclical net interest margin compression as ECB policy rates decline. Under the Mauboussin framework, commercial banking is anchored in Tier 4 with rapid return fade (baseline CAP 5-10 years). Operating in a saturated Spanish domestic market with low economic growth and demographic headwinds in core rural regions, CAP cannot exceed 5 years.
column21: Historical capital returns have been modest and cyclical: ROTE was 4.7% in 2023, recovering to 10.4% in 2024 and 9.1% standard / 12.1% adjusted in 2025 as higher interest rates boosted net interest income. Cost-to-income ratio stands at ~44-46%. Balance sheet is heavily weighted toward domestic residential mortgages (~60% of loans), where pricing is largely commoditized against Santander, BBVA, and CaixaBank. Post-merger governance friction and domestic Spanish sovereign exposure further curtail long-term predictability.

column14: Sticky retail and SME deposit franchise creates primary-bank switching costs in core cantons, but pricing power is constrained by commoditized mortgage lending and competition from state-backed Cantonal banks.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). Swiss regional retail and SME bank expanding outside core Bernese cantons into competitive markets. Lacks scale, technological differentiation, or pricing power against state-guaranteed Cantonal banks and nationwide institutions, facing secular margin compression in commoditized mortgage lending.
column21: Valiant operates as a regional Swiss retail bank with ROE of ~5.7%, well below cost of equity hurdles. High capital intensity and credit/deposit duration risks without an enduring structural competitive advantage over 15+ years.

column14: World's #3 reinsurer with the lowest admin cost ratio (~1.5%) in the global industry; passes cost efficiencies to ceding clients to secure preferred treaty access while maintaining disciplined risk-adjusted underwriting.
column20: Top-tier global reinsurer with industry-leading low-cost operations. Passes Gate 6: real cash conversion, 16%+ median ROIC, float-funded business model, and pristine Solvency II capital buffer above 250%. [5-10Y g: P&C reinsurance volume 3.5% + treaty rate hardening 2.0% + investment float yield 1.0% + capital return 0.5%]
column21: 5-year median ROIC of 16.0%, EBIT growing from €1,525M (2022) to €3,546M (2025), and Solvency II ratio of 256%-261% well above the 200% threshold. Operating cost advantage and conservative reserve redundancy provide multi-cycle underwriting resilience.

column14: Unrivaled balance sheet scale and proprietary actuarial data enable underwriting of complex mega-risks; scale economies and ERGO integration create superior risk absorption and hard market pricing leverage.
column20: The world's leading reinsurance powerhouse. Passes Gate 6: genuine cash generation, multi-decade unbroken dividend, 20%+ median ROIC, and fortress balance sheet with ~298% Solvency II ratio and massive negative-cost float. [5-10Y g: reinsurance volume 3.0% + price indexation 2.0% + ERGO direct growth 1.0% + buybacks 1.0%]
column21: 5-year median ROIC of 20.5%, Net Income compounding to record €6,118M in FY2025, interest coverage >24x, and Solvency II ratio of 287%-298% (far exceeding the 200% threshold). Reserving prudence placed in the top decile of global peers.

column20: Fails Gate 1 (Understandability / Outside Verifiability, REJECT). Long-tail Life & Health reinsurance assumptions and casualty reserving are opaque and unverifiable from the outside. In 2024, unexpected negative experience variances forced severe actuarial assumption revisions, wiping out group net income to €4M and requiring external actuarial firms (Milliman, WTW) to audit book values.
column21: SCOR incurred ~€0.7B in pre-tax insurance service result hits and a ~€1.3B CSM downward adjustment in 2024 due to legacy life reinsurance assumption revisions. Chronic reserve volatility and reliance on complex biometric/mortality actuarial estimates violate Gate 1 external verifiability.

column20: Fails Gate 1 (Understandability / Outside Verifiability, REJECT). Opaque long-tail US liability and casualty reinsurance reserving with multi-billion-dollar retroactive reserve additions ($3.1B in 2024 alone following $2.0B in 2023) demonstrating that true underwriting profitability and economic risk exposure cannot be verified from the outside by an equity investor.
column21: Swiss Re added $3.1B to prior-year US casualty reserves across the first nine months of 2024 (including a $2.4B charge in Q3 2024) to address social inflation and litigation severity, following $2.0B of reserve strengthening in 2023. These repeated large-scale reserve shocks highlight long-tail casualty reserving opacity under Gate 1(b).

column14: Single-stack proprietary tech eliminates intermediary fees and maximizes authorization rates; tiered volume pricing (scale economies shared) cements enterprise lock-in with negligible churn.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. The world's most advanced single-stack global payments platform with pristine owner-operator leadership, >€10B net cash fortress, and compounding owner earnings. [5-10Y g: processed volume 14.0% - tiered volume take-rate step-down 4.0% + unified commerce and platforms expansion 2.0%]
column21: Capital-light single stack generating 25%+ ROE, operating ROIC >200%, Owner EPS compounding from €18.17 in 2022 to €33.93 in 2025, >€10B cash balance with minimal debt, and industry-leading authorization rate outperformance.

column14: Two-sided B2B platform connecting fund managers and wealth distributors benefits from operational integration and administrative switching costs. However, it lacks genuine pricing power: institutional fund managers and private banks exert constant fee pressure, and statutory GAAP ROIC is sub-12% (averaging ~8%) weighed down by heavy post-IPO capitalized goodwill and intangibles.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% and lack of pricing power). B2B mutual fund distribution platform suffers from structural active-to-passive industry migration, persistent take-rate fee compression from institutional asset managers, and sub-hurdle GAAP ROIC (~8%) burdened by historical capitalized goodwill.
column21: Reported GAAP net income of €49.2M in 2022 and €85.7M in 2023 yielded GAAP ROIC of ~8%, failing the 12% hurdle. In 2024, statutory results swung to a net loss of €168.5M due to discontinued operations and separately disclosed items. Platform take rates face perpetual downward renegotiation from fund managers coping with passive ETF outflows, demonstrating an inability to raise prices at or above inflation.

column14: Multi-sided meal voucher and employee benefits network connects corporate employers, employees, and merchants with high employer switching costs. However, it structurally lacks pricing power: the business model relies on state tax incentives, provoking merchant revolt and statutory government fee caps (e.g. Italy's 5% merchant commission cap under Law 193/2024 and ongoing French regulatory scrutiny) that permanently compress take rates.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Zero pricing power due to statutory fee caps and antitrust intervention). Meal voucher and corporate benefits platform rests on tax privileges rather than unassisted economic value; extreme merchant resentment has triggered statutory commission caps (such as Italy's 5% cap enacted in 2024/2025) and ongoing antitrust investigations in France and Italy, permanently capping take-rate pricing power.
column21: Italy implemented Law 193/2024 capping merchant voucher commissions at 5% (down from historical 15-25%), severely cutting core Italian EBITDA and triggering AGCM antitrust investigations into alleged circumvention fees. The French Competition Authority has historically fined the sector for cartel behavior and continues regulatory reviews. Because voucher take rates are vulnerable to legislative caps and merchant litigation, Edenred cannot pass through inflation-linked fee increases.

column14: Merchant acquiring and card issuing network benefits from bank-partner distribution and Italian domestic scale, but lacks pricing power against modern platforms (Adyen, Stripe) and fails on sub-8% GAAP ROIC resulting from massive debt-funded goodwill (Nets and SIA mergers).
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% and lack of pricing power). Legacy European payment processor created via debt-funded rollups (Nets, SIA); suffers from sub-hurdle GAAP ROIC (~5-7%), billions in goodwill, high financial leverage (~€5.2B net debt), and persistent take-rate pressure from modern competitors like Adyen.
column21: GAAP ROIC averages ~5-7%, severely depressed by ~€18B-19B in invested capital following the Nets and SIA mergers. Statutory results saw heavy impairments and low net income (€171M in 2024 vs large net loss in 2023). High net debt of €5.2B (2.7x EBITDA) limits financial flexibility while merchant acquiring faces secular fee compression from tech-native payment platforms.

column14: Nick Sleep / Costco flywheel in cross-border payments: Wise passes scale efficiencies directly back to customers via lower take rates (~0.60% vs legacy banks at 2-3%), driving massive volume growth and 25%+ ROE while widening its competitive moat.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. The undisputed cost leader in global cross-border payments, using a Munger scale-economies-shared flywheel to disrupt legacy banks. Direct integrations with central bank payment rails yield an unassailable unit cost advantage, founder-led culture of radical transparency, and fortress balance sheet with over £12B in cash/customer balances and minimal net corporate debt. [5-10Y g: cross-border volume 15.0% - price/fee reduction 3.0% + Wise Business account mix 3.0% - rate income fade 1.0% + share repurchases 0.0%]
column21: Revenue compounded from £1,052M in FY2024 to £1,212M in FY2025 with Profit Before Tax reaching £565M and net profit £417M. Tangible ROE exceeds 25-30% on corporate capital. Low capex requirements (<£30M) yield FCF conversion exceeding 100% of net income. Direct connections to central bank settlement systems (UK Faster Payments, Australia NPP, Europe SEPA) create a structural cost floor that commercial banks cannot match without cannibalizing high-margin legacy fee structures.

column20: Fails Gate 1 (Pre-commercial clinical biotech). Zero product revenue; enterprise value hinges entirely on binary clinical and regulatory trial outcomes for single lead drug candidate obefazimod in ulcerative colitis.
column21: Pre-revenue clinical-stage biotechnology company with net losses expanding from €182M in 2024 to €336M in 2025 as Phase 3 trials progress. Generates no commercial product sales, lacking an established economic engine or multi-cycle operating track record.

column14: Patented FcRn antagonist platform (Vyvgart / efgartigimod) enjoys high clinical switching costs and neurologist brand equity in generalized myasthenia gravis (gMG) and CIDP. High orphan pricing ($225k+/year) and rapid commercial adoption generated >$4B in 2025 product sales, swinging GAAP ROIC to >25%. However, long-term persistence faces direct competing FcRn biologics (J&J nipocalimab, UCB rozanolixizumab) and finite patent runway.
column20: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 5, REJECT). Single-product commercial biotech relying almost entirely on Vyvgart (>95% of revenues). Under the Mauboussin persistence framework, biotech is Tier 3 (10-15Y baseline), and faces sharp haircuts due to near-term FcRn competition from mega-pharma rivals (J&J nipocalimab, UCB Rystiggo) and primary patent expirations in the early 2030s, capping the Competitive Advantage Period at 5 years (well below the 15-year threshold).
column21: While Vyvgart commercial sales scaled rapidly to $2.2B in 2024 and $4.2B in 2025 generating $1.29B in net profit, argenx's 5-year median GAAP ROIC is -6.1% due to clinical-stage cash burn before 2024. More crucially, revenue is overwhelmingly concentrated in a single molecule whose primary composition-of-matter patents expire around 2031-2033. Aggressive competing FcRn entrants (J&J, UCB, Immunovant) and bio-similar threats prevent confidence in a 15+ year durable competitive advantage period.

column14: Pioneering antibody discovery platform (DuoBody, HexaBody), but Genmab acts primarily as a royalty taker on J&J's Darzalex without independent pricing power, facing an imminent 2029 US patent cliff.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Genmab is an antibody engineering pioneer but operates primarily as a contractual royalty recipient on J&J's Darzalex (accounting for 65-80%+ of revenue). It possesses zero independent pricing power to increase royalty rates above inflation and faces a major unhedged 2029 US patent cliff after losing legal arbitration on Darzalex Faspro.
column21: Genmab's high historical GAAP ROIC (>20%) is heavily distorted by passive royalties on Johnson & Johnson's Darzalex sales. Genmab has no discretion over realized drug pricing, which faces mandatory Medicare IRA price negotiations in the US and statutory cuts in Europe. With core Darzalex US patents expiring in 2029 and EU in 2031, Genmab faces severe revenue and margin compression, forcing costly defensive pipeline M&A (e.g., ProfoundBio for $1.8B) that expands invested capital while high-margin royalty streams evaporate.

column20: Fails Gate 1 (Rejected – G1 Understandability). Opaque accounting disclosures, labyrinthine related-party governance structures involving family-controlled vehicle Scranton Enterprises NV, dual-consolidation of plasma assets (Haema, BPC Plasma), and disputed true leverage fail Charlie Munger's circle of competence and external verifiability standards.
column21: Despite holding a strong position in plasma fractionation and plasma-derived therapies, Grifols' reported financials violate the Gate 1 verifiability test. Investigations triggered by Gotham City Research reports and subsequent CNMV regulatory reviews revealed complex related-party financial structures, call-option sale-and-leaseback mechanisms with Scranton Enterprises, and non-transparent adjustments that masked actual leverage (estimated real net debt/EBITDA of 10-13x versus stated ~6x).

column14: Rare disease portfolio (hematology/immunology) built largely via debt-fueled in-licensing and acquisitions rather than proprietary discovery, resulting in bloated intangibles and severe product write-downs.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Sobi lacks an enduring organic R&D moat, relying on debt- and equity-fueled acquisitions to mask structural patent expirations in core hemophilia assets. Capital allocation missteps—epitomized by the SEK 17.1B acquisition of CTI BioPharma followed by a massive SEK 6.6B impairment on Vonjo in 2025—depress multi-cycle GAAP ROIC well below the 12% hurdle.
column21: Sobi's rare disease commercialization model has suffered heavy capital misallocation: the acquisition of CTI BioPharma underperformed commercially, forcing a SEK 6,612M pre-tax write-down in 2025 that crushed operating profit to SEK 867M and net income to SEK 478M. On an invested capital base bloated by goodwill and intangible rights (>SEK 35B), GAAP ROIC fell to low single digits in 2025, pulling 5-year median GAAP ROIC below the 12% requirement. Flagship hemophilia drugs (Elocta, Alprolix) face ongoing technological substitution.

column20: Fails Gate 1 (Rejected – G1 Understandability). Pre-commercial, clinical-stage biotechnology company whose valuation and lumpy revenue hinge almost entirely on binary Phase 3 clinical trial outcomes (petrelintide, survodutide) and upfront partnership milestones rather than an established multi-cycle commercial operating track record.
column21: Zealand Pharma has operated historically as a clinical-stage development biotech generating chronic operating losses (e.g., 2024 net loss of DKK -1.08B on only DKK 63M commercial revenue). Although 2025 accounting net income surged to DKK 6.46B due to one-off upfront licensing milestone fees from Roche, the company lacks an established commercial sales engine. Its enterprise value remains exposed to binary regulatory approval and clinical trial execution risks in the hyper-competitive GLP-1/amylin obesity therapeutic arena.

column14: Dominant Swiss pharmacy network and wholesale distribution infrastructure (Galexis/Alloga), but sub-hurdle 10% ROIC and triennial statutory FOPH/BAG drug price cuts prevent raising prices above inflation.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Dominant Swiss pharmacy network and healthcare distributor with resilient volumes, but 5-year median ROIC of 10.0% falls strictly below the 12% hurdle. Furthermore, triennial statutory drug price cuts and regulated dispensing margins mandated by the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH/BAG) permanently cap pricing power below inflation.
column21: Galenica generates consistent but structurally sub-hurdle returns on capital across 2021-2025: reported ROIC has ranged tightly between 9.2% and 10.1% (5-year median 10.0%, failing the >=12% test). Core prescription medicine revenue is subject to statutory price reviews by the Swiss FOPH (BAG) that enforce structural price cuts across reimbursable medicines, limiting top-line pricing power despite retail service expansion and generic substitution buffers.

column14: Installed base of ophthalmic surgical consoles mandates high-margin closed-system consumables per surgery with steep surgeon switching costs, complemented by annual 3-5% price hikes and premium mix in contact lenses.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global eye care titan leading ophthalmic surgical equipment/consumables and contact lenses. Moat anchored in massive installed console base driving recurring single-use consumable sales and surgeon workflow lock-in. 16%+ operating ROIC and >100% FCF conversion overcome legacy Novartis spin-off intangibles. [5-10Y g: cataract/contact lens volume 4.5% + AT-IOL/SiHy price-mix 2.0% + operating leverage 1.5% + share buybacks 0.5%]
column21: Global #1 in ophthalmic surgical equipment and #2 in vision care. Operating ROIC of 16-18% comfortably clears hurdles (GAAP ROIC depressed by ~$18B legacy Novartis spin-off PPA intangibles). Multi-year Owner FCF conversion exceeds 100% ($1.45B Owner FCF vs $980M net income in 2025). Net debt of $2.6B is 2.7x net income, and interest coverage is 6.7x EBIT. Demographically insulated from all 5 macrotrends with aging populations driving cataract surgery volumes.

column14: ~85% proprietary recurring reagents and high-value multiplex panels (BioFire, VITEK) enable inflation pass-through while sustaining >55% gross margins with near-zero hospital lab churn.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global in vitro diagnostics leader in clinical microbiology and syndromic PCR (BioFire) with ~85% recurring reagent revenues. High switching costs in hospital labs sustain >55% gross margins and >16% operating ROIC. Balance sheet is an unleveraged net cash fortress. [5-10Y g: installed-base & panel volume 5.0% + reagent price/mix 1.5% + operating leverage 1.0%]
column21: Operating ROIC consistently 15.3%–24.1% (median 16.4%). 2025 Owner FCF of €454.8M on €397.5M Net Income (114% conversion; 4-year cumulative €1,177M FCF on €1,640M NI following post-COVID capex normalization). Closed-system instrument footprint (VITEK, BACT/ALERT, FilmArray) locks in ~85% recurring reagent sales across hospital laboratories globally. Balance sheet holds €358M net cash with 34x interest coverage.

column14: Oligopoly hearing aid R&D scale and owned retail clinic network, but severe channel pricing power headwinds (VA, NHS, Costco), consumer electronics substitution (Apple AirPods), and capital-destroying M&A write-downs (SteelSeries, Oticon Medical exit) prevent sustainable >12% ROIC and real pricing power above inflation.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Proof of Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT). Hearing aid oligopoly faces persistent channel pricing pressure from institutional payers (VA, NHS) and big-box retail (Costco), along with rising consumer tech substitution (Apple AirPods Pro OTC hearing features). Multi-cycle ROIC fails the consistent >=12% Munger bar following dilutive acquisitions and restructuring.
column21: Multi-cycle GAAP ROIC hovers around 8%–13% with volatile trough periods (5.3% in 2020, 8.6% in 2022). Capital allocation track record marred by the ill-fated acquisition of gaming headset maker SteelSeries and the costly exit and divestment of Oticon Medical. Retail hearing care expansion and prescription hardware face continuous pricing erosion from institutional procurement tenders and direct-to-consumer alternatives.

column14: Unmatched end-to-end vertical integration from proprietary corrective lens technology (Varilux, Stellest) to iconic frame brands (Ray-Ban, Oakley) and 18,000+ retail stores sustains ~63% gross margins and immense consumer pricing power.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Colossus of the global optical industry with unrivaled vertical integration across corrective lenses (Varilux, Stellest), iconic frames (Ray-Ban, Oakley), and global retail. High pricing power sustains ~63% gross margins and 140%+ FCF conversion. [5-10Y g: vision-care & myopia volume 3.5% + progressive lens/smart-glasses price-mix 2.5% + margin expansion 1.0%]
column21: Tangible operating ROIC exceeds 85% (GAAP ROIC ~6% reflects €41B+ merger intangibles). Exceptional multi-year Owner FCF conversion of 140.8% (€3.49B FCF on €2.32B Net Income in 2025). Monopolistic vertical integration spanning 18,000 retail doors (LensCrafters, GrandVision), proprietary lens technology, and Ray-Ban Meta AI smart glasses. Net debt repayable in <2 years with 11.2x interest coverage.

column14: Severe hospital GPO tender price competition and chronic manufacturing quality failures (decade-long FDA consent decree, 2024 FDA transition advisory, CE mark suspensions) have crushed pricing power, driven customer defection, and impaired returns on capital.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Proof of Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT). Chronic quality management failures—including a decade-long FDA consent decree, repeated Class I recalls, a 2024 FDA advisory urging hospitals to replace Getinge cardiac/ECMO devices, and CE mark suspensions—demonstrate severe structural moat erosion and inability to sustain economic pricing power.
column21: Sub-hurdle multi-cycle ROIC and continuous remediation charges. Over 3,000 Medical Device Reports tied to Cardiosave IABP prompted an unprecedented FDA letter advising clinicians to migrate to alternative suppliers, eroding Getinge's market share in cardiopulmonary and acute care hardware and culminating in the planned 2025 wind-down of its traditional heart-lung machine line.

column14: Installed imaging base and patient monitoring contracts, but catastrophic Respironics foam recall, FDA/DOJ consent decree halting US sleep device production, massive multi-billion-dollar legal liabilities, and market share losses to ResMed, Siemens, and GE have shattered pricing power and depressed ROIC below hurdles.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Proof of Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT). The catastrophic Respironics recall and 2024 DOJ/FDA consent decree eliminated US sleep device sales, inflicted over $2.5B in legal settlements, and permanently ceded market share to ResMed. Multi-cycle GAAP ROIC is deeply sub-hurdle (<6%) amid fierce imaging competition from Siemens and GE.
column21: Multi-year GAAP ROIC severely depressed by multi-billion-dollar recall provisions, litigation payouts ($1.08B personal injury, $500M economic loss, €288M DOJ settlement), and goodwill write-downs. High-margin sleep and respiratory revenue was largely halted in the US under federal court order, while medical imaging equipment faces fierce tender discounting against Siemens Healthineers and GE HealthCare.

column14: Global gold standard in radiology and pathology imaging IT (#1 KLAS for 11+ years); 7-10 year CPI-indexed SaaS contracts and exam-volume pricing produce near-zero churn and >75% median GAAP ROIC.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Elite owner-operated medical imaging IT and digital pathology leader with an unrivaled customer satisfaction record (#1 KLAS for 11+ years). Mission-critical hospital workflow lock-in and CPI-indexed SaaS contracts generate 75%+ ROIC, >120% cash conversion, and a massive net cash fortress. [5-10Y g: cloud SaaS & new hospital wins 7.0% + exam volume & digital pathology 2.5% + CPI price indexation 1.5% + margin expansion 0.5%]
column21: Astronomical GAAP ROIC (median 75.5%, FY2025 >100%) and 122.8% multi-year FCF conversion. SEK 1.75B net cash balance sheet with 98x interest coverage. Flawless execution across hospital enterprise imaging transitions (radiology, cardiology, digital pathology) with industry-leading #1 Best in KLAS rating for 11 consecutive years and near-zero customer defection.

column14: Installed base of >600,000 systems creates deep clinical and software switching costs, generating ~45% recurring high-margin service revenue. Technological lead in photon-counting CT and Varian radiation oncology monopolies protect pricing power across hospital procurement cycles.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global duopoly in medical imaging (MRI/CT) and monopoly in radiation oncology (Varian). Deep workflow switching costs with ~45% recurring high-margin service revenue. Solid ~8x interest coverage and ~97% FCF conversion. [5-10Y g: Imaging/Varian volume 4.5% + price/mix 1.5% + margin/deleverage 1.5%]
column21: Median GAAP ROIC 13.2% (tangible ROIC >20%), FCF conversion ~97%. Over €23B in revenues with dominant market shares in advanced therapies, MRI/CT, and linear accelerators. 8.1x EBIT interest coverage with net debt/EBITDA ~1.2-1.5x.

column14: Surgeon switching costs and regulatory clearances exist in theory, but chronic execution failures and persistent market share loss in reconstruction (knees and hips) to Stryker and Zimmer Biomet demonstrate weak moat. Multi-year ROIC of 6.6-8.3% persistently misses the 12% hurdle.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%, REJECT). Multi-cycle ROIC languishes at 6.6-8.3%, well below the 12% cost-of-capital threshold. Chronic operational execution missteps, supply chain friction, and persistent market share loss in orthopedic implants to Stryker and Zimmer Biomet show lack of moat pricing power.
column21: Adjusted ROIC of 6.6% (2022), 7.4% (2024), and 8.3% (2025) fails the 12% hurdle. Operating margins under pressure from procurement and supply-chain challenges, trailing peers Stryker and Zimmer Biomet across hip/knee reconstruction.

column14: Loss of Costco Kirkland contract, US managed-care/Medicare Advantage intermediary ASP squeeze, and entry-level commoditization from OTC hearing aids and Apple AirPods Pro compress real pricing power and margins.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power, REJECT). While Sonova maintains strong DSP audiology engineering, pricing power is structurally compromised by FDA OTC hearing-aid deregulation, Apple AirPods Pro encroaching at 1/10th the cost ($250 vs $3k+), and managed-care/Costco wholesale channel pricing pressure.
column21: Operating margins under multi-year pressure from channel shifting toward discount/managed care and loss of the Costco Kirkland contract. Regulatory OTC deregulation and Big Tech consumer audio integration permanently cap entry-level hearing aid ASPs.

column14: Single-payer government price-taker. US Medicare ESRD Prospective Payment System dictates fixed reimbursement rates, completely stripping pricing power. Multi-year ROIC of 2.8-5.0% fails the 12% hurdle by a wide margin.
column20: Fails Gate 3a/3b (No Moat / Zero Pricing Power, REJECT). Dialysis clinic operations are captive to government reimbursement price caps (Medicare ESRD PPS), eliminating pricing power while nurse wage inflation compresses margins. Multi-year ROIC of 2.8-5.0% fails the 12% hurdle by a wide margin.
column21: Reported ROIC of 2.8% (2023), 3.5% (2024), and 5.0% (2025). Severe margin compression from US clinical labor shortages and fixed statutory Medicare reimbursement schedules. Long-term treatment volumes pressured by GLP-1 kidney disease progression delay.

column14: Hospital network density (Helios) and IV generics manufacturing scale (Kabi) fail to generate economic rents. Regulated hospital DRG reimbursement schedules, statutory staffing mandates, and generic drug procurement GPOs severely compress pricing power, yielding sub-7% ROIC.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%, REJECT). Multi-cycle ROIC of 5.2-6.6% languishes far beneath the 12% cost-of-capital bar. Hospital operations (Helios) face severe German DRG pricing regulation and clinical wage inflation, while Kabi IV generics lack pricing power against hospital purchasing cartels.
column21: Reported group ROIC of 5.2% (2023), 6.2% (2024), and 6.6% (2025) persistently fails the 12% hurdle despite FME deconsolidation and #FutureFresenius cost-cutting programs.

column14: Global #1 in ostomy (~38-40% share) and continence care (~40% share). Enormous switching costs driven by stoma nurse training and intimate patient loyalty against leakage/infection. Sustained 19%+ GAAP ROIC and 27-30% EBIT margins via recurring consumable replacement and premium innovation tiers (SenSura Mio, Luja).
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global market leader in ostomy (~40%) and continence (~40%) consumables. Unmatched switching costs rooted in nurse recommendations and patient dependence on leak-free intimate care. Excellent ~19% GAAP ROIC, ~87% FCF conversion, and manageable 2.4x EBITDA leverage. [5-10Y g: organic volume 5.5% + price/mix 1.5% + margin recovery 0.5%]
column21: Median GAAP ROIC 19.2% (tangible >50%), FCF conversion ~87%. Global market share leader in ostomy and continence care. Daily disposable consumable replacement model provides rock-solid recession resilience. 6.85x EBIT interest coverage with Net Debt/EBITDA at 2.4x.

column14: #2-#3 positions in ostomy and advanced wound care face intense hospital GPO tenders and single-payer reimbursement ceilings, holding GAAP ROIC to 7-9%, far below leader Coloplast.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). While ConvaTec provides essential chronic-care supplies (ostomy, infusion sets, advanced wound care), it holds #2-#3 market positions behind Coloplast and Hollister. Sub-12% GAAP ROIC (~7-9%) and vulnerability to hospital GPO tenders and Medicare reimbursement pressure demonstrate inadequate pricing power.
column21: ConvaTec generated reported operating margins of 12.3% in 2023 and 14.2% in 2024 (adjusted margins ~20-21%), with historical GAAP ROIC hovering in the 7-9% range, well below the 12% threshold. Its ostomy and wound care segments face persistent reimbursement caps from European single-payers and US Medicare/GPO contract cycles, lacking the brand premium and margin insulation of market leader Coloplast.

column14: Global #1 dental implant franchise (~32% market share) backed by deep clinician switching costs (ITI training ecosystem), 75% gross margins, and 20-30%+ GAAP ROIC. Premium SLActive/BLX pricing and Neodent value tier offset localized pricing pressures.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Global #1 dental implant and digital dentistry leader with high clinician switching costs and 75% gross margins. Structural demographic tailwinds from population aging offset dental cyclicality and China VBP. Fortress net-cash balance sheet with >30x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: organic implant/digital volume 6.5% + premium price/mix 1.5% + operating leverage 1.0% + net buybacks 0.0%]
column21: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 30.0% and tangible ROIC of 67.9% demonstrate an exceptional economic moat. Straumann commands ~32% global market share in dental implants, underpinned by clinician lock-in via the ITI network and proprietary surface technologies (SLActive, Roxolid). Multi-year FCF conversion averages 87.9%. Net cash position of CHF 225M (CHF 475M cash vs CHF 250M debt) and 30x+ interest coverage provide balance sheet peace of mind through consumer dental cycles.

column14: Regulatory CMC spec-in lock-in across ~75%+ recurring consumables supports pricing power and ~28-30% normalized EBITDA margins.
column20: Fails Gate 5 (Management & Capital Allocation = 0, REJECT). Strong FDA/EMA-validated single-use bioprocessing moat ruined by top-of-cycle debt-funded M&A (€2.4B Polyplus) and subsequent dilutive €1.2B equity raise to pay down debt, reflecting poor capital allocation discipline by parent-controlled management.
column21: Sartorius Stedim Biotech holds an enviable competitive moat in single-use bioprocessing consumables with high regulatory switching costs. However, management severely destroyed shareholder value in 2023 by acquiring Polyplus for €2.4B near the peak of the cell-therapy bubble, pushing leverage to ~4.5x EBITDA. In February 2024, management was forced to execute a dilutive €1.2B capital increase at depressed share prices to pay down parent-company debt, demonstrating egregious capital allocation and disregard for per-share compounding.

column14: Competitive food/environmental testing and French clinical diagnostics fee cuts prevent full inflation pass-through, resulting in sub-hurdle 6-9% GAAP ROIC diluted by hundreds of roll-up acquisitions.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). Broad bioanalytical testing network fails to generate hurdle returns, with multi-year GAAP ROIC mired at 6-9% due to heavy roll-up goodwill. Inability to pass through 2022-2023 wage/energy inflation and clinical tariff cuts prove insufficient pricing power.
column21: Eurofins operates an extensive global network of over 900 laboratories across food, environmental, and clinical testing. However, reported GAAP ROIC has persistently averaged between 6.7% and 8.9% (below the 12% hurdle), diluted by endless small-scale M&A. When wage and energy inflation hit in 2022-2023, operating margin contracted to ~8.4%, showing lack of pricing power amidst regulated clinical reimbursement tariffs and fragmented competition.

column14: Mission-critical biologics CDMO site validation creates switching barriers, but extreme capex intensity (20-30% of sales) and industry batch lumpy utilization depress median GAAP ROIC to 7.9%.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Pricing Power, REJECT). World-leading biologics CDMO with high regulatory site validation switching barriers, but structural heavy capex intensity (CHF 1.4-1.9B annually) and cyclical capacity utilization trap multi-year GAAP ROIC at 7.9%, well below the 12% threshold.
column21: Lonza's reported GAAP ROIC has averaged 7.86% over the last four years (11.8% in 2022, 6.8% in 2023, 6.3% in 2024, 8.9% in 2025). The CDMO business model requires relentless capital reinvestment (capex representing 20-30% of revenue, including large facility acquisitions like Vacaville), leaving capital efficiency chronically depressed below the cost of capital.

column14: Dominant #1 global share in sample preparation (>60%) and standard-of-care QuantiFERON-TB testing lock in lab workflows, supporting ~66% gross margins, >34% tangible ROIC, and steady annual price realization.
column20: Passes all 6 gates. Unassailable global leader in molecular sample preparation and QuantiFERON latent-TB diagnostics, generating >85% recurring consumable revenues. Tangible ROIC >34% and multi-year FCF conversion >100%. COVID windfall normalized with core non-COVID business compounding peak-to-peak. Modest leverage (net debt <2x earnings) and >15x interest coverage. [5-10Y g: sample-prep/QuantiFERON volume 4.5% + price 1.5% + portfolio mix 0.5% + net share buybacks 1.0%]
column21: QIAGEN holds a ~60-70% global market share in biological sample preparation (DNA/RNA extraction) and gold-standard status with QuantiFERON-TB. Tangible ROIC has consistently exceeded 30% (median 34.2%), and FCF conversion averaged 128% over the last four years. Post-pandemic normalization of COVID testing windfalls is complete, with 2025 sales ($2.09B) and net income ($425M) well above pre-COVID 2019 levels ($1.53B and $338M). Balance sheet is sound with $815M net debt repayable in <2 years and interest coverage of 15.7x.

column14: Regulatory cGMP switching barriers and tech-transfer stickiness exist, but heavy plant capex and competitive small-molecule CDMO market keep 5-year median ROIC ~8-9%, well below the 12% threshold.
column20: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12%, REJECT). Reliable Swiss CDMO with regulatory switching barriers in API synthesis and sterile fill-finish, but high plant capex and competitive small-molecule pricing keep 5-year median ROIC below 9%, failing the 12% hurdle.
column21: Reported Core EBITDA margins run ~21-23% and Core EBIT margins ~15-16%, but multi-year post-tax GAAP ROIC averages only ~8-9% due to heavy tangible capital bases (plants in Minden, Hameln, Pennsville) and working capital intensity. Fails 12% ROIC requirement.

column14: Validated bioprocess consumables (single-use bioreactor bags, sterile filters, chromatography media) embedded into regulatory biologic drug filings create insurmountable customer switching barriers and high cycle-average ROIC.
